questions.stem: A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being thrown from his motorcycle onto asphalt. After his clothing is removed, a red, raw lesion is noted running along the lateral aspect of his left leg and forearm, which he calls "road rash." There is no deep bleeding, and only the most superficial layers of skin appear to have been scraped away. Which of the following best classifies this injury?

explanation.summary: An abrasion is removal of the superficial layers of skin by friction or compression.
explanation.whyCorrect: Abrasions remove the top layers of skin through friction or compression, as with a "skinned" area of road rash after being dragged across pavement. There is no deep hemorrhage or penetration, consistent with loss of only the superficial skin.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A contusion is hemorrhage into soft tissue from ruptured blood vessels (a bruise) with the surface typically intact, not a scraping away of skin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An incised wound is a sharp cut or slash that is longer than it is deep, produced by a sharp edge rather than friction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A laceration is a tearing of tissue by blunt shearing or crushing forces and classically shows tissue bridging, which is absent here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A stab wound is penetration by a pointed object with depth greater than width, not a superficial surface scrape.

questions.topicName: Environmental Disease Part 2 of 2: Physical Agents

questions.stem: A 20-year-old man collapses near the end of a marathon on a hot, humid afternoon. He is confused and combative. His rectal temperature is 41.5 C (106.7 F). Which of the following findings would be most specific for his diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Heat stroke reflects failure of thermoregulation, marked by profound mental status changes and cessation of sweating.
explanation.whyCorrect: In heat stroke the core temperature rises above 40 C (104 F) and thermoregulation ceases, so sweating stops. Combined with profound mental status changes, cessation of sweating is the finding most specific for thermoregulatory failure.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cramping muscles occur with heat cramps from loss of electrolytes during sweating and are not specific for heat stroke.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Decreased blood volume from sweating-related hypovolemia characterizes heat exhaustion and can be seen in several heat illnesses, so it is not specific.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Erythema of the skin is a nonspecific finding that can be seen in many settings.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Shortness of breath is nonspecific and does not distinguish heat stroke from other conditions.

questions.topicName: Environmental Disease Part 2 of 2: Physical Agents

questions.stem: A 68-year-old farmer with decades of outdoor sun exposure develops a scaly, ulcerated lesion on his lower lip; biopsy shows squamous cell carcinoma. The ultraviolet B radiation responsible for this malignancy characteristically causes which of the following forms of DNA damage?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reactive oxygen species from radiolysis of water

explanation.summary: UVB, a nonionizing radiation, is carcinogenic through pyrimidine dimer formation in DNA.
explanation.whyCorrect: UVB exerts its carcinogenic effect by causing the formation of pyrimidine dimers, with covalent cross-linking of adjacent thymidine residues. This nonionizing mechanism underlies UV-associated skin cancers.

whyWrongByChoice.A: DNA-protein crosslinks result from ionizing radiation rather than ultraviolet exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Double-stranded DNA breaks are a form of direct damage caused by ionizing radiation, not UV light.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reactive oxygen species generated by radiolysis of water are an indirect mechanism of ionizing radiation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Single-stranded DNA breaks are among the direct DNA injuries produced by ionizing radiation.

questions.topicName: Environmental Disease Part 2 of 2: Physical Agents

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman is evaluated after a house fire. One burn on her forearm appears pale, waxy, and mottled. It does not blanch with pressure, but she can perceive deep pressure and pin-prick sensation over the area. Which of the following best classifies this burn?

explanation.summary: Deep partial-thickness burns reach the reticular dermis and appear pale, waxy, and mottled with retained deep-pressure sensation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Deep partial-thickness burns extend into the reticular dermis, producing a pale, waxy, mottled appearance that does not blanch. Pressure or pin-prick sensation from intact deep Pacinian corpuscles may still be felt, exactly as described.

whyWrongByChoice.A: "Chemical burn" describes a cause of injury from a corrosive substance, not a depth of thermal injury.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Full-thickness burns extend into fat below the dermis and are painless with a leathery eschar, not a mottled dermis with retained sensation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Superficial (first-degree) burns are confined to the epidermis, are erythematous and painful, blanch to touch, and do not blister.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Superficial partial-thickness burns involve the papillary dermis and are red, blistering, painful, and blanch to touch.

questions.topicName: Environmental Disease Part 2 of 2: Physical Agents

questions.stem: A construction worker sustains a burn on his thigh from prolonged contact with a hot metal surface. The area is dry, leathery, and white, and he reports no pain when the wound is examined. Which of the following best explains the absence of pain in this burn?

choices.label: E
choices.text: The superficial location of the injury

explanation.summary: Full-thickness burns are painless because destruction of tissue extends deep enough to destroy nerves.
explanation.whyCorrect: A dry, leathery, white appearance with a firm eschar indicates a full-thickness (third-degree) burn extending into the fat below the dermis. These burns are painless due to destruction of the nerves within the injured tissue.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The epidermis is destroyed in a full-thickness burn, not intact.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Vasoconstriction of dermal vessels does not account for the loss of pain sensation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Endorphin release is not the mechanism the source attributes to painlessness in these burns.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The injury is deep, not superficial; superficial burns are in fact painful.

questions.topicName: Environmental Disease Part 2 of 2: Physical Agents

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man has a circumferential full-thickness burn encircling his entire right forearm. Over several hours the forearm becomes increasingly tense and firm, and the distal radial pulse weakens. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Application of a tourniquet proximal to the forearm

explanation.summary: A circumferential eschar can compromise limb circulation (compartment syndrome), treated by escharotomy.
explanation.whyCorrect: An eschar that encompasses the circumference of an extremity can compromise blood supply, causing increased soft tissue pressures, ischemia, and compartment syndrome. Escharotomy is the surgical opening of the wound to relieve pressure and restore blood flow.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A tourniquet would further reduce distal perfusion and worsen ischemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A fasciotomy opens the fascia and is directed at the affected limb; a fasciotomy of the uninjured lower leg does not address the forearm eschar.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Amputation is not the appropriate first step for a threatened but salvageable limb with rising compartment pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anticoagulation does not relieve the mechanical constriction produced by a circumferential eschar.

questions.topicName: Environmental Disease Part 2 of 2: Physical Agents

questions.stem: A 35-year-old electrician grasps a live wire and is unable to release it because of sustained muscle contraction. He is found pulseless and unresponsive. Which of the following is a recognized principal mechanism of death from electrocution?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Crystallization of intracellular water in frozen tissue

choices.label: B
choices.text: Disruption of the cardiac conduction system

choices.label: C
choices.text: Excessive collagen deposition during wound healing

choices.label: D
choices.text: Formation of pyrimidine dimers in epidermal DNA

choices.label: E
choices.text: Radiolysis of intracellular water generating free radicals

explanation.summary: Electrocution kills through disruption of cardiac conduction, disruption of neuronal activity, or asphyxia from respiratory muscle paralysis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Electrical injury can produce ventricular fibrillation and cardiac arrest by disrupting the cardiac conduction system, one of the three principal mechanisms of death by electrocution. Alternating household current also causes muscle spasm that prevents release of the wire.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Crystallization of intracellular water mediates tissue damage in hypothermia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Excessive collagen deposition causes hypertrophic scarring after burns, not electrocution death.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pyrimidine dimer formation is the mechanism of UVB radiation injury, not electrocution.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Radiolysis of water generating reactive oxygen species is a mechanism of ionizing radiation.

questions.topicName: Environmental Disease Part 2 of 2: Physical Agents

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man treated months earlier with external-beam radiation therapy for a head and neck tumor develops progressive firmness of the irradiated tissue and reduced salivary flow. Histologic examination of the region shows narrowing of small blood vessels. Which of the following best explains this vascular change?

explanation.summary: Vessels are sensitive to radiation and undergo narrowing through fibrointimal thickening, with surrounding tissue fibrosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Radiation damage makes vessels undergo narrowing through fibrointimal thickening, and attempts at repair throughout affected tissues commonly result in widespread fibrosis. This accounts for both the vessel narrowing and the firm, poorly functioning irradiated gland.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amyloid deposition is not the radiation-associated mechanism of vessel narrowing.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Caseating granulomas are characteristic of infections such as tuberculosis, not radiation-induced vascular change.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fatty streaks are early atherosclerotic lesions unrelated to the fibrointimal response described after radiation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neutrophilic vasculitis reflects an inflammatory vasculitis rather than the fibrosing vascular injury of radiation.

questions.topicName: Environmental Disease Part 2 of 2: Physical Agents

questions.stem: A 15-month-old child who recently began walking is brought to clinic after being noted to limp. Radiographs reveal a spiral fracture of the distal tibia. There is no other evidence of injury, and the history is consistent with an ordinary fall for a child of this age. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this fracture?

explanation.summary: A toddler's fracture is a non-abusive spiral fracture of the distal tibia that may occur when a child is learning to walk.
explanation.whyCorrect: Not all pediatric spiral fractures are abusive. The toddler's fracture is a non-abusive spiral fracture of the distal tibia that occurs as a child learns to walk and may present without an inciting event beyond the common everyday falls of this age group.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Although spiral fractures can raise concern for abuse, an isolated distal tibial spiral fracture in a new walker with a consistent history and no other injuries favors a toddler's fracture.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Osteogenesis imperfecta typically produces multiple or recurrent fractures with other features such as blue sclerae, not described here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A pathologic fracture from malignancy would be expected to show an underlying bony lesion, which is not present.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rickets causes bony deformities and metaphyseal changes rather than an isolated spiral fracture from a minor fall.

questions.topicName: Environmental Disease Part 2 of 2: Physical Agents

questions.stem: A forensic pathologist examines a scalp wound with irregular margins. Strands of intact tissue are seen crossing the depth of the wound. Which of the following types of injury is most consistent with this finding?

explanation.summary: Tissue bridging is a classic sign of a laceration (blunt tearing) and is not expected in a sharp injury.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tissue bridging, in which strands of tissue span the depth of the wound, is a classic sign of a laceration caused by blunt shearing or crushing forces. Distinguishing a laceration from an incised wound is important in a criminal investigation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An abrasion is a superficial removal of skin by friction, not a deep wound with bridging strands.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A contusion is hemorrhage into intact soft tissue (a bruise) rather than an open wound.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Incised wounds are produced by a sharp edge, are longer than they are deep, and show clean margins without tissue bridging.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Stab wounds are sharp penetrating injuries that are deeper than they are wide and do not exhibit tissue bridging.

questions.topicName: Environmental Disease Part 2 of 2: Physical Agents

questions.stem: A man experiencing homelessness is brought to the emergency department after a night spent outdoors in freezing weather. Several of his fingertips are hard, black, and shriveled with a mummified appearance. Which of the following best describes this finding?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Heat-related tissue necrosis from a burn

explanation.summary: Severe frostbite causes deep tissue necrosis manifesting as dry gangrene with black mummification.
explanation.whyCorrect: Frostbite is the freezing of tissue. Severe cases with deep injury result in necrosis, an example of dry gangrene that appears as black mummification of the affected part.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The injury results from freezing (cold), not heat.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hypertrophic scarring is an excessive collagen response seen in wound healing after burns, not cold injury.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Limited frostbite appears pale and waxy with development of bullae and blisters, not black mummified tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Paradoxical undressing is a behavior seen in hypothermia in which victims remove clothing before death, not a description of tissue appearance.

questions.topicName: Environmental Disease Part 2 of 2: Physical Agents

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy with poorly controlled asthma lives in an older, poorly maintained home. On a home visit his physician notes visible mold on the walls and observes that the child's symptoms worsen indoors. Growth of this mold is most directly promoted by which of the following aspects of the indoor environment?

explanation.summary: Damp, humid indoor air promotes mold growth, a socioeconomic environmental factor linked to respiratory disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Damp and humid indoor air contributes to mold growth, which is associated with a wide variety of respiratory symptoms, including asthma-related disease. Indoor environment is an important environmental factor with socioeconomic implications.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Carbon monoxide is a poisonous gas from incomplete combustion; it does not cause mold growth.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Excessive cold is not the factor that drives mold growth in the home.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dryness inhibits rather than promotes mold growth.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Excessive heat is not associated with the mold growth described here; moisture is the key factor.

questions.topicName: Environmental Disease Part 2 of 2: Physical Agents

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman with newly diagnosed lung cancer undergoes a full staging workup. The report lists a 3-cm primary tumor, involvement of two regional lymph nodes, grade 3 (anaplastic) histology, and a solitary lesion in the liver consistent with tumor spread. Which of the following findings most strongly worsens her prognosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A tumor that is well vascularized

choices.label: B
choices.text: Involvement of two regional lymph nodes

choices.label: D
choices.text: The 3-cm size of the primary tumor

explanation.summary: Distant metastasis (the M in TNM) is the single most important component of staging and confers the worst prognosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Of the three TNM components, metastasis is the most important prognostic factor, and spread to a distant organ such as the liver carries the worst outlook. It outweighs tumor size, nodal spread, and grade.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Vascularity of the tumor is not one of the prognostic parameters emphasized in staging and grading.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Nodal involvement (N) ranks below metastasis in prognostic weight; two nodes is less severe than distant spread.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tumor size (T) is the least important of the three TNM components and is far less ominous than distant spread.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Grade is an important prognostic factor but is explicitly less important than stage, and metastasis dominates staging.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man completes chemotherapy for lymphoma. On follow-up, his physical exam, blood work, and imaging show no evidence of cancer, and the oncologist says he is in complete remission. Which of the following best describes what this means?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All signs and symptoms of the cancer have disappeared

choices.label: B
choices.text: Imaging shows no growth of the original tumor, though symptoms persist

choices.label: C
choices.text: Signs and symptoms are alleviated but not eliminated

choices.label: D
choices.text: The cancer has been definitively cured and cannot return

choices.label: E
choices.text: The tumor is at least 50% smaller than before treatment

explanation.summary: Complete remission means all evidence, signs, and symptoms of cancer have disappeared, but it is not the same as cure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Complete remission means no cancer is detectable on physical exam, blood work, or imaging. It is distinguished from cure because undetected cancer cells may still remain and could regrow.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Imaging showing no growth of the original tumor with residual disease describes partial remission, not complete remission.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Signs and symptoms alleviated but not eliminated defines partial remission.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Providers avoid the word cure because undetected cells may persist even in complete remission; complete remission is not a guarantee of cure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A tumor at least 50% smaller but still present is a criterion for partial remission, not complete remission.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman is diagnosed with breast cancer. Her oncologist tells her that, based on her diagnosis, 75% of patients with her cancer will not die as a result of their cancer within 5 years of diagnosis. Which parameter is the oncologist using to describe her prognosis?

choices.label: D
choices.text: 5-year relative survival versus a matched population

explanation.summary: Cancer-specific survival counts only deaths caused by the cancer itself over a set period after diagnosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cancer-specific survival is the percentage of patients with a specific type and stage who have not died as a result of that specific cancer in a given period after diagnosis. That is exactly what the oncologist described.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Disease-free survival is the percentage with no signs of cancer during a period after completing treatment, not deaths from the cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Overall survival counts patients who have not died from any cause, not just the cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Relative survival compares survival of patients with cancer to a matched cancer-free population.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The oncologist specified a 5-year window and death from the cancer, not a 10-year overall figure.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: A biopsy of a breast mass is reviewed by a pathologist. Which of the following histologic descriptions most likely corresponds to a high-grade cancer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cells that form glands and resemble normal breast tissue

choices.label: C
choices.text: Extensive tumor infiltration into adjacent tissue and lymph nodes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Poorly differentiated cells with numerous mitoses

explanation.summary: Grade reflects histology; high-grade tumors are poorly differentiated or anaplastic with marked nuclear atypia and abundant mitoses.
explanation.whyCorrect: Grade describes the histologic appearance and number of mitoses. High-grade (poorly differentiated or anaplastic) cancers lack differentiation, show pleomorphic nuclei, and have numerous mitotic figures.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cells that form glands and resemble normal tissue describe a well-differentiated, low-grade tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Serum tumor marker levels are not a component of grade, which is based on microscopic appearance.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Infiltration into adjacent tissue and lymph nodes reflects stage (extent of spread), not grade.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Well-differentiated cells with uniform nuclei describe a low-grade, not a high-grade, cancer.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man has an elevated serum CA19-9 detected during evaluation of abdominal pain and weight loss. An elevation of this tumor marker is most classically associated with which of the following cancers?

explanation.summary: CA19-9 is a tumor marker associated with colon and pancreatic cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: CA19-9 is classically elevated in pancreatic cancer (and colon cancer). In a patient with abdominal pain and weight loss, a high CA19-9 points toward pancreatic cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hepatocellular carcinoma is marked by alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), not CA19-9.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Neuroendocrine tumors are associated with chromogranin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ovarian cancer is associated with CA-125.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prostate cancer is associated with prostate-specific antigen (PSA).

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with non-small cell lung cancer is assigned a stage of T2 N1 M1. Which single feature of his cancer carries the greatest weight in determining his prognosis?

choices.label: C
choices.text: The moderate differentiation of the tumor

choices.label: D
choices.text: The N1 involvement of one lymph node

explanation.summary: Among the three TNM components, metastasis (M) is the most important prognostic factor.
explanation.whyCorrect: The M component describes distant spread and is the most important of the three TNM factors. M1 (metastasis present) therefore weighs most heavily on prognosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Tumor markers help track response and recurrence but are not the dominant prognostic component of TNM staging.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Grade (differentiation) is a prognostic factor but is less important than stage.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nodal involvement (N) is important and second to metastasis, but still ranks below M.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tumor size (T) is the least important of the three TNM components.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman is diagnosed with stage 3B non-small cell lung cancer. Using the staging-based survival data, which of the following is closest to her expected 5-year survival rate?

explanation.summary: Higher stage means worse prognosis; stage 3B non-small cell lung cancer has roughly a 5% 5-year survival.
explanation.whyCorrect: The stage-specific survival table lists a 5-year survival of about 5% for stage 3B non-small cell lung cancer, illustrating how advancing stage sharply lowers survival.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 1% corresponds to stage 4 (metastatic) disease, worse than stage 3B.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 14% corresponds to stage 3A disease, one substage below 3B.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 31% corresponds to roughly stage 2B disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 49% corresponds to stage 1A disease, much earlier than stage 3B.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: A researcher reports that, for a particular cancer, a given statistic represents the percentage of patients with that cancer type and stage who have not died from any cause within 5 years of diagnosis. Which survival measure is being described?

explanation.summary: Overall survival counts patients who have not died from any cause during a set period after diagnosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Overall survival is the percentage of patients with a specific type and stage of cancer who have not died from any cause in a certain period after diagnosis, which matches the description exactly.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cancer-specific survival counts only deaths caused by the cancer, not deaths from any cause.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Disease-free survival tracks the absence of cancer signs after completing treatment, not death from any cause.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Progression-free interval is not one of the survival measures defined in the source.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Relative survival compares patients with cancer against a matched cancer-free population.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man treated for colorectal carcinoma had a carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) level that normalized after surgery. During surveillance, his CEA begins to rise steadily on serial measurements. Which of the following does this trend most likely suggest?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A normal age-related change in the marker

choices.label: B
choices.text: A positive response to ongoing treatment

choices.label: E
choices.text: That the patient is now cured

explanation.summary: After a baseline is established following treatment, a rising tumor marker suggests cancer recurrence.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tumor markers are useful for monitoring after treatment. Once a post-treatment baseline is set, a later increase in the marker suggests the cancer has returned.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The PSA example, not CEA, is the marker described as changing with age; a steady rise here reflects disease, not aging.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A decrease in a tumor marker, not an increase, signifies a positive treatment response.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Complete remission requires no detectable cancer; a rising marker indicates the opposite.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A rising marker argues against cure; providers are already reluctant to use the term cure.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with advanced cancer has progressive weakness, loss of appetite, and marked muscle wasting with more than 5% loss of body weight despite adequate nutrition offered. This hypercatabolic state is thought to account for roughly 30% of cancer deaths. Which of the following mediators are most implicated in this process?

explanation.summary: Cancer cachexia is a hypercatabolic wasting state driven by inflammatory mediators such as TNF, IL-1, and IL-6.
explanation.whyCorrect: The picture describes cancer cachexia, a hypercatabolic state with loss of muscle mass that occurs in about half of cancer patients and contributes to roughly 30% of cancer deaths. Inflammatory mediators including TNF, IL-1, and IL-6 are implicated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: AFP and CEA are tumor markers, not cytokines driving cachexia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Estrogen and progesterone are hormones related to breast cancer biology, not drivers of cachexia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Insulin and glucagon regulate glucose metabolism and are not the implicated inflammatory mediators.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PSA and CA-125 are tumor markers, not mediators of the wasting process.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman receives chemotherapy for cancer. Follow-up imaging shows her tumor burden has decreased by about 60% with no new lesions, but residual tumor is still present and blood tests remain mildly abnormal. Which of the following terms best describes her current status?

explanation.summary: Partial remission means the cancer responded to treatment and shrank, but signs of disease remain.
explanation.whyCorrect: Partial remission means signs and symptoms are alleviated but not eliminated; imaging showing tumors at least 50% smaller and not growing, with residual disease, fits partial remission.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cancer-specific survival is a population survival statistic, not a status for an individual's tumor response.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Complete remission requires that all evidence, signs, and symptoms have disappeared, but residual tumor remains here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cure means no trace of cancer at all, which is not the case with visible residual tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Disease-free survival is a survival statistic measured after treatment completion, not a description of current tumor response.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman is diagnosed with breast cancer, and molecular testing is performed to help refine her prognosis. Which of the following receptor profiles is associated with the most favorable prognosis?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Presence of both BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations

explanation.summary: In breast cancer, estrogen receptor-positive and HER2/Neu-negative tumors carry a better prognosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Molecular characteristics influence prognosis: estrogen receptor-positive breast cancers carry a better prognosis than receptor-negative ones, and HER2/Neu-negative cancers carry a better prognosis than HER2/Neu-positive ones. The combination of both favorable features is the most favorable profile.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Estrogen receptor-negative removes the favorable receptor feature, worsening prognosis relative to receptor-positive disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Estrogen receptor-negative and HER2/Neu-positive combines two unfavorable features and has a worse prognosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HER2/Neu-positive status is unfavorable and offsets the benefit of being receptor-positive.
whyWrongByChoice.E: BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations are molecular features that can worsen prognosis and are not the favorable receptor profile described.

questions.topicName: Cancer Staging and Grading

questions.stem: In an animal model, a renal artery is clamped briefly and then released. A biopsy taken during the clamp shows tubular epithelial cells that are swollen with pale, watery cytoplasm; the nuclei appear intact, and the swelling resolves after blood flow is restored. Which of the following best explains the reversible swelling of these cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deposition of homogeneous pink hyaline protein

choices.label: D
choices.text: Release of lysosomal DNases digesting the nucleus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rupture of the plasma membrane with loss of cellular contents

explanation.summary: Cellular swelling is the classic morphologic change of reversible injury and stems from ATP depletion.
explanation.whyCorrect: When hypoxia depletes ATP, the Na+/K+ pumps that maintain osmotic balance can no longer be powered, so ions and water accumulate and the cell swells. Because this is early and the stimulus is transient, restoring ATP returns the cell to normal osmotic balance, making swelling the hallmark of reversible injury.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hyaline change is an intracellular protein accumulation, not the mechanism of acute swelling.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Karyorrhexis is a nuclear change of cell death, not the cause of reversible swelling.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Leakage of lysosomal enzymes reflects membrane damage in irreversible injury.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Plasma membrane rupture is a hallmark of irreversible injury, not a reversible change.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: A cardiac myocyte is subjected to prolonged, severe hypoxia. Which of the following morphologic findings would most reliably indicate that the injury has become irreversible?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Restoration of normal osmotic balance after reoxygenation

explanation.summary: Membrane rupture is a defining feature of irreversible cellular injury.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that a major defining feature of irreversible injury is membrane rupture, which allows leakage of cellular contents and, when lysosomal membranes fail, releases destructive enzymes. Once the membrane is breached the cell cannot recover.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytoplasmic swelling is the classic change of reversible injury.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mild, reversible mitochondrial swelling does not by itself signal irreversibility.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Recovery of osmotic balance after reoxygenation indicates the injury was reversible.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A transient volume increase is a reversible osmotic change.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: A 20-month-old infant is found to have a retinoblastoma driven by biallelic inactivation of the RB tumor-suppressor gene. When the pathologist identifies this loss-of-function mutation as the event that initiated the disease, which core aspect of pathologic inquiry is being described?

explanation.summary: Etiology is the initiating cause of a disease, which is typically genetic or environmental.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines etiology as the initiation of disease, often a genetic event such as an inherited or acquired mutation. Biallelic RB inactivation is the genetic event that starts the tumor, making it the etiology.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Clinical manifestations are the observed results, such as leukocoria on examination.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Morphologic changes are the microscopic findings such as poorly differentiated cells and rosettes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pathogenesis is the mechanism by which the unchecked cell cycle leads to tumor growth, not the initiating cause.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prognosis refers to the expected disease course, such as the favorable survival rate.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: A firefighter is pulled unconscious from a burning building. Cyanide poisoning from smoke inhalation is suspected. Cyanide injures cells primarily by which of the following mechanisms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activating lysosomal proteases at the plasma membrane

choices.label: D
choices.text: Generating free radicals through ionizing radiation

explanation.summary: Cyanide blocks mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase, halting aerobic ATP production.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that cyanide, a product of incomplete combustion, inhibits mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase and thereby inhibits oxidative phosphorylation, decreasing ATP production through aerobic respiration. This energy failure is what damages cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cyanide's target is the mitochondrial electron transport chain, not lysosomal proteases.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Injury tends to raise cytosolic calcium; cyanide does not primarily deplete calcium stores.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cyanide does not act by directly cross-linking DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ionizing radiation, not cyanide, generates free radicals that cause oxidative stress.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: A patient's occluded coronary artery is successfully reopened. Paradoxically, myocardial tissue damage worsens after blood flow is restored. Which of the following best explains this ischemia-reperfusion injury?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A sudden fall in systemic calcium levels

choices.label: B
choices.text: Continued complete absence of oxygen delivery

choices.label: D
choices.text: Returning blood delivers oxygen and inflammation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reversal of anaerobic glycolysis to aerobic respiration

explanation.summary: Reperfusion can worsen injury because restored blood brings oxygen and inflammatory cells that generate ROS.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that restoring blood flow not only brings nutrients but also an influx of oxygen and inflammation that lead to ROS-mediated injury of the already stressed tissue. This is the mechanism of ischemia-reperfusion injury.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ischemia-reperfusion injury is driven by ROS, not by a drop in systemic calcium.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Reperfusion restores, rather than continues to withhold, oxygen delivery.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glycogen depletion is not the described mechanism of reperfusion injury.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A return to aerobic respiration is beneficial and does not explain the added damage.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: Aerobic cells continuously produce superoxide, a reactive oxygen species. Which of the following enzymes catalyzes the first step of neutralizing superoxide by converting it into hydrogen peroxide?

explanation.summary: Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide, the first step in radical scavenging.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes that superoxide is converted to hydrogen peroxide by superoxide dismutase, and that hydrogen peroxide is then further converted to water by glutathione peroxidase and catalase. Superoxide dismutase performs the initial conversion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Catalase acts downstream, converting hydrogen peroxide to water, not superoxide.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cytochrome oxidase is a mitochondrial electron-transport enzyme, not a radical scavenger.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glutathione peroxidase also acts on hydrogen peroxide, a later step.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lactate dehydrogenase functions in anaerobic glycolysis, not radical detoxification.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man has had a blood pressure of 160/100 mm Hg for several years without treatment. Which of the following cellular adaptations is most likely present in his myocardium?

explanation.summary: Chronic pressure overload causes cardiac myocytes to enlarge (hypertrophy).
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that hypertrophy is an increase in cell size from increased protein production in response to functional demand, such as cardiac muscle facing an increased workload. Because muscle cells cannot replicate, the heart adapts to sustained hypertension by enlarging its existing myocytes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atrophy is a response to decreased demand, the opposite of the increased workload here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hyperplasia requires cell division, but cardiac muscle cells cannot replicate.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Metaplasia is a change of one cell type to another and does not occur in the heart in this setting.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sustained hypertension produces a definite adaptive change over time.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: A postmenopausal woman on unopposed estrogen therapy presents with abnormal uterine bleeding. An endometrial biopsy shows an increased number of endometrial glands compared with normal tissue. Which cellular adaptation does this represent?

explanation.summary: Excess estrogen stimulation increases endometrial cell number, producing hyperplasia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that hyperplasia is an increase in cell number, and that pathologic hyperplasia from excess estrogen stimulation causes endometrial hyperplasia, which can present clinically as abnormal uterine bleeding. The increased number of glands reflects added cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atrophy is a decrease in cell size or number, the opposite of what is seen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dystrophic calcification is calcium deposition in damaged tissue, unrelated to glandular proliferation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hypertrophy is an increase in cell size, not cell number.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Metaplasia is replacement of one cell type by another, not an increase in glands.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: A long-term smoker undergoes bronchial biopsy, which shows the normal ciliated columnar respiratory epithelium replaced by tougher stratified squamous epithelium. This change is best described as which of the following?

explanation.summary: Replacement of one differentiated epithelium by another is metaplasia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that metaplasia is a reversible change in which one differentiated cell type is replaced by another, using the example of tobacco smoke inducing metaplasia of ciliated columnar respiratory epithelium into more resistant squamous cells. Removing the stimulus can reverse the change.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anthracosis is accumulation of black carbon pigment, not a change in epithelial type.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Atrophy is a decrease in cell size or number.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyperplasia is an increase in cell number, not a switch in cell type.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hypertrophy is an increase in cell size.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: At autopsy of an elderly patient, hard, chalky deposits are found within a heavily damaged, atherosclerotic aortic valve. Review of records shows the patient's serum calcium and phosphate were normal. This calcification is best classified as which of the following?

explanation.summary: Calcification of damaged tissue with normal serum calcium is dystrophic calcification.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines dystrophic calcification as deposition occurring in damaged tissues under normal systemic calcium homeostasis, using the example of a damaged, atherosclerotic aortic valve. Normal serum calcium plus locally damaged tissue fits this definition.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemosiderin is an iron-rich blood-breakdown pigment, not calcification.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyaline change is a pink, glassy protein accumulation, not a calcium deposit.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lipofuscin is a brown wear-and-tear pigment of aging, not a calcium deposit.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Metastatic calcification deposits in otherwise normal tissue due to hypercalcemia, such as excess parathyroid hormone; serum calcium here is normal.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: A pathologist examines the heart of an elderly patient and notes a brown, granular pigment accumulating within cardiomyocytes. The pigment is composed of oxidized proteins and lipids, builds up with age particularly in non-dividing cells, and is not harmful to the cell. Which pigment is this?

explanation.summary: Lipofuscin is the brown wear-and-tear pigment of aging, seen in non-dividing cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes lipofuscin as a brown wear-and-tear pigment of proteins and lipids that accumulates with aging, particularly in non-dividing cells such as skeletal muscle, neurons, and cardiomyocytes, and notes it is not harmful to cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anthracotic pigment is inhaled black carbon that accumulates in the lung and lymph nodes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bilirubin is a yellow-brown bile pigment from abnormal bile excretion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemosiderin is a yellow-brown iron pigment from blood breakdown, not an aging pigment of oxidized lipids.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Melanin is a brown-black pigment produced by melanocytes.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: To estimate how rapidly a lymphoma is proliferating, a pathologist orders a stain in which antibodies target a cell-cycle antigen, turning positive nuclei brown. Which of the following techniques is being used?

explanation.summary: Ki-67 immunohistochemistry uses antibodies against a cell-cycle antigen to estimate proliferation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that immunohistochemistry deploys antibodies against a protein of interest, staining it brown or red, and that Ki-67 is an immunostain targeting an antigen involved in the cell cycle used to estimate cellular proliferation. Brown nuclear positivity in a lymphoma is a classic Ki-67 result.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Eosin stains proteins in the cytoplasm pink and is not a proliferation marker.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hematoxylin stains nucleic acids blue-purple but does not measure cell-cycle activity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: H&E shows general morphology but does not specifically quantify proliferation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PAS-D highlights substances such as glycogen or alpha-1 antitrypsin globules, not proliferation.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Pathology, Cell Injury, and Adaptation

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man collapses with crushing substernal chest pain and dies before reaching the hospital. At autopsy, a firm, pale, wedge-shaped area is seen in the left ventricular wall. On microscopy the myocytes in this region retain their cellular outlines but have lost their nuclei, and the underlying tissue architecture is preserved. Which pattern of necrosis is most consistent with these findings?

explanation.summary: Ischemic infarction of a solid organ such as the heart produces coagulative necrosis, in which tissue architecture is preserved.
explanation.whyCorrect: Coagulative necrosis results from loss of blood supply (ischemia) and is defined by preservation of the underlying tissue architecture of the dead cells. A localized area of coagulative necrosis is an infarct, classically seen as a firm, pale wedge in the heart after a myocardial infarction, where anucleate myocytes still retain their outlines.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Caseous necrosis produces friable, cheese-like debris within a granuloma and is associated with tuberculosis, not ischemic myocardium.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fat necrosis produces chalky-white saponified deposits from lipase action on adipose tissue, as in pancreatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fibrinoid necrosis is a pattern of vessel-wall injury with deposited fibrin and immune complexes, not a myocardial infarct pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Liquefactive necrosis digests dead cells into a viscous liquid and does not preserve tissue architecture; it is characteristic of the central nervous system, not the heart.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: An autopsy of a 69-year-old man with a history of atherosclerosis reveals an infarct of brain parenchyma perfused by the middle cerebral artery. The affected region is softened and has been converted into a fluid-filled cavity. Which type of necrosis is most closely associated with his cause of death?

explanation.summary: Ischemia within the central nervous system produces liquefactive necrosis, converting dead tissue into a liquid.
explanation.whyCorrect: Liquefactive necrosis is dominated by digestion of dead cells, resulting in a viscous liquid of necrotic material and inflammatory cells. Unlike other organs where ischemia causes coagulative necrosis, ischemia in the central nervous system results in liquefactive necrosis, leaving a fluid-filled cavity at the infarct site.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Caseous necrosis shows a cheese-like appearance and is associated with tuberculosis and other granulomatous infections, not a bland brain infarct.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Coagulative necrosis, in which architecture is retained, is the pattern of ischemia in most solid organs but NOT in the brain.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fibrinoid necrosis reflects immune-mediated vascular wall damage, not liquefaction of infarcted brain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gangrenous necrosis is a clinical term applied to ischemic death of a limb or digits, not brain tissue.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man presents with several weeks of productive cough, night sweats, and weight loss. A chest CT shows an upper-lobe lung lesion. Biopsy demonstrates granulomas with a central area of friable, off-white material that grossly resembles cheese. Which pattern of necrosis is present?

explanation.summary: The cheese-like appearance of necrotic debris within a granuloma is caseous necrosis, classically caused by tuberculosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The term caseous refers to the friable, cheese-like, off-white appearance of the necrotic material. Under the microscope, ample fragmented and granular debris is enclosed within a granuloma. Caseous necrosis is commonly associated with tuberculosis infection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Coagulative necrosis preserves tissue architecture after ischemia and lacks the cheese-like granulomatous debris.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fat necrosis produces chalky-white calcium/fatty-acid deposits in adipose tissue, as in pancreatitis, not granulomas.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fibrinoid necrosis is a vessel-wall pattern with fibrin and immune complexes, not a lung granuloma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Liquefactive necrosis creates a liquid or pus and is typical of CNS ischemia or bacterial abscess, not caseating granulomas.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man with heavy alcohol use is admitted with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and a markedly elevated serum lipase. During surgery, the surgeon notes multiple firm, chalky-white deposits scattered across the fat of the peritoneal cavity. Which process best explains these deposits?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deposition of fibrin and immune complexes in vessel walls

choices.label: B
choices.text: Digestion of dead cells into a viscous liquid

choices.label: D
choices.text: Preservation of tissue architecture after ischemia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Saponification of fatty acids with calcium

explanation.summary: In acute pancreatitis, released lipases digest adipose tissue and fatty acids combine with calcium to form chalky-white deposits (fat necrosis).
explanation.whyCorrect: Fat necrosis occurs with breakdown of adipose tissue. In acute pancreatitis, pancreatic lipases leak into the fat-rich peritoneal cavity, and the released fatty acids combine with calcium to produce a chalky-white substance in a process called saponification. Hard, basophilic calcium deposits are seen microscopically.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fibrin and immune-complex deposition in vessel walls describes fibrinoid necrosis of vasculitis, not the chalky fat deposits of pancreatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Digestion into a viscous liquid describes liquefactive necrosis, seen in CNS infarcts and abscesses.
whyWrongByChoice.C: BCL2 overexpression blocks apoptosis and drives follicular lymphoma; it has nothing to do with pancreatic fat necrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Preservation of architecture after ischemia describes coagulative necrosis, which does not produce saponified fat.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with granulomatosis with polyangiitis undergoes renal biopsy for hematuria and rising creatinine. Microscopy of a small artery shows the vessel wall replaced by a bright pink, amorphous material containing deposited fibrin and immune complexes, with associated thrombosis. Which pattern of necrosis does this represent?

explanation.summary: Deposition of fibrin and immune complexes within an injured vessel wall is fibrinoid necrosis, seen in vasculitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fibrinoid necrosis refers to a pattern of severe vascular injury in which fibrin and immune complexes deposit in the vessel wall, producing a bright pink appearance. It is seen in vasculitis and autoimmune diseases targeting blood vessels, such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Caseous necrosis produces cheese-like granulomatous debris associated with tuberculosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Coagulative necrosis is the pattern of ischemic infarcts in solid organs and preserves tissue architecture rather than depositing fibrin in vessel walls.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fat necrosis produces chalky saponified deposits in adipose tissue, as in pancreatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gangrenous necrosis is a clinical term for ischemic death of a limb or digits.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with long-standing poorly controlled diabetes mellitus is evaluated for several black, shriveled toes. The affected digits are dry, mummified, and mottled, and the changes extend across multiple tissue planes. There is no purulent discharge. Which term best describes this pattern of tissue death?

explanation.summary: Ischemic death of a limb or digits that crosses multiple tissue planes and appears mummified is gangrenous necrosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gangrenous necrosis refers to ischemic tissue death of a limb, such as the lower leg or digits, that involves multiple tissue planes. It may appear mummified or rotting. When dry, as in this patient, it lacks the wet, liquefied quality that results from bacterial degradative enzymes and host inflammation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Caseous necrosis is the cheese-like debris of granulomatous infection such as tuberculosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fat necrosis produces chalky saponified deposits in adipose tissue, as in pancreatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fibrinoid necrosis is a microscopic vessel-wall pattern in vasculitis, not a gross description of dead toes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Liquefactive necrosis produces a viscous liquid or pus and is classically seen with CNS ischemia or bacterial abscess, not dry mummified toes.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: In response to irreparable DNA damage, a cell releases a protein from its mitochondria into the cytoplasm. This protein forms an apoptosome complex that binds and activates a critical initiator caspase, launching the executioner caspase cascade. Which caspase is activated by this mitochondrial (intrinsic) pathway?

explanation.summary: In the intrinsic pathway, cytochrome c forms an apoptosome that activates caspase-9.
explanation.whyCorrect: When the outer mitochondrial membrane becomes permeable, cytochrome c is released into the cytoplasm, where it forms an apoptosome complex. This complex binds caspase-9, the critical executioner-initiating caspase of the intrinsic pathway, which then triggers a cascade of downstream executioner caspases.

whyWrongByChoice.A: BAX is a pro-apoptotic effector that permeabilizes the outer mitochondrial membrane but does not act as the activated caspase.
whyWrongByChoice.B: BCL2 is an anti-apoptotic protein that prevents cytochrome c release; it is not a caspase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Caspase-8 is the initiator caspase of the extrinsic (death receptor) pathway, activated through FADD, not by the apoptosome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: FADD is the adaptor protein of the extrinsic pathway that recruits caspase-8; it is not a caspase itself.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man has painless generalized lymphadenopathy. Lymph node biopsy shows a follicular pattern, and cytogenetics reveal a t(14;18) translocation that places the BCL2 gene adjacent to the immunoglobulin heavy-chain enhancer, causing BCL2 overexpression. Which mechanism best explains how this abnormality promotes tumor growth?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enhanced caspase-8 activation through the Fas death receptor

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excessive fibrin deposition within lymph node vessels

choices.label: C
choices.text: Failure of apoptosis due to sustained blockade of cytochrome c release

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased outer mitochondrial membrane permeability with cytochrome c release

choices.label: E
choices.text: Uncontrolled necrosis with spillage of cellular contents

explanation.summary: Overexpressed BCL2 keeps the mitochondrial membrane impermeable, blocking apoptosis so that lymphoma cells accumulate.
explanation.whyCorrect: Anti-apoptotic proteins such as BCL2 keep the outer mitochondrial membrane impermeable, preventing release of cytochrome c and blocking the intrinsic apoptotic pathway. In follicular lymphoma, t(14;18) places BCL2 under the immunoglobulin heavy-chain enhancer, causing overexpression that pathologically prevents apoptosis and facilitates lymphoma growth and proliferation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enhanced caspase-8 activation would increase death receptor apoptosis, not allow tumor cells to survive.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fibrin deposition in vessels describes fibrinoid necrosis of vasculitis and is unrelated to BCL2.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased permeability with cytochrome c release would promote apoptosis, the opposite of what BCL2 overexpression does.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Necrosis is uncontrolled death from injury and is not the mechanism by which BCL2 overexpression drives lymphoma.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A cytotoxic T lymphocyte recognizes a virus-infected cell and engages the target cell's Fas receptor using Fas ligand. Clustering of Fas causes the cytoplasmic death domains to form a binding site for an adaptor protein, which in turn activates an initiator caspase. Which protein is directly activated at this step of the extrinsic pathway?

explanation.summary: In the extrinsic pathway, Fas clustering recruits FADD, which activates caspase-8.
explanation.whyCorrect: When Fas ligand on a cytotoxic T cell binds Fas, the receptors cluster and their cytoplasmic death domains form a binding site for FADD (Fas-associated death domain). FADD leads to the activation of caspase-8, which then initiates the executioner caspase cascade. Caspase-8 can also cleave BID to recruit the intrinsic pathway.

whyWrongByChoice.A: BAX is a pro-apoptotic effector of the intrinsic pathway, not the initiator caspase of the death receptor route.
whyWrongByChoice.B: BCL2 is an anti-apoptotic protein of the intrinsic pathway and is not activated by death receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Caspase-9 is activated by the apoptosome in the intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway, not directly by FADD.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cytochrome c is released by mitochondria in the intrinsic pathway and is not the caspase activated by Fas.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman with metastatic melanoma begins treatment with pembrolizumab, an antibody directed against the PD-1/PD-L1 axis. Immunohistochemistry of her tumor had shown high PD-L1 expression. Which statement best describes how this drug helps eliminate the tumor?

choices.label: B
choices.text: It directly triggers coagulative necrosis of the tumor mass

choices.label: C
choices.text: It increases tumor BCL2 expression to promote cell survival

choices.label: D
choices.text: It inhibits caspase-9 to prevent apoptosis of host T cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: It stimulates tumor PD-L1 to enhance immune tolerance

explanation.summary: Checkpoint inhibitors block the PD-1/PD-L1 interaction so cytotoxic T cells can again drive apoptosis of tumor cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: PD-L1 expressed on tumor cells binds PD-1 on T cells and blocks T-cell attack, allowing immune evasion. Checkpoint inhibitors such as pembrolizumab and nivolumab block this interaction, preventing PD-1/PD-L1 binding and restoring the T cell's ability to kill the cancer cell through apoptosis. PD-L1 immunohistochemistry helps select patients for this therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The drug works by unleashing immune-mediated apoptosis, not by directly inducing coagulative necrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Increasing BCL2 would block apoptosis and protect the tumor, the opposite of the intended effect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The drug targets the PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint, not caspase-9, and its goal is to promote tumor cell death rather than inhibit apoptosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Stimulating PD-L1 would enhance immune evasion, not treat the cancer.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A pathologist is comparing two histologic specimens. In the first, isolated single cells are shrunken with dense eosinophilic cytoplasm and fragmented nuclei, surrounded by intact neighboring cells and no inflammatory infiltrate. Which feature best identifies this process as apoptosis rather than necrosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A significant surrounding inflammatory cell infiltrate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cell shrinkage with a preserved plasma membrane and no inflammation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Random degradation of DNA throughout the injured tissue

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rupture of the plasma membrane with spillage of cell contents

choices.label: E
choices.text: Swelling of groups of adjacent cells with karyolysis

explanation.summary: Apoptosis affects single cells with shrinkage, maintained membrane integrity, and no inflammation, distinguishing it from necrosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Apoptotic cells undergo shrinkage rather than swelling, with dense eosinophilic cytoplasm and controlled nuclear breakup. Membrane integrity is maintained as the cell blebs into apoptotic bodies that phagocytes ingest, so there is no robust inflammatory response. In contrast, necrosis affects groups of cells with swelling, membrane rupture, and significant inflammation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A significant inflammatory reaction accompanies necrosis, whereas apoptosis provokes little to none.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Random DNA degradation is seen in necrosis; apoptosis shows ordered internucleosomal fragmentation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Membrane rupture with spilled contents is a hallmark of necrosis; apoptotic membranes remain intact.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Swelling of groups of adjacent cells is characteristic of necrosis, not apoptosis.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A medical student is asked to identify which of several processes represents physiologic apoptosis rather than pathologic necrosis. Which of the following is best classified as physiologic apoptosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bowel wall death from mesenteric ischemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cardiomyocyte death after coronary artery occlusion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hepatocyte death from severe thermal burn injury

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neuronal death following a middle cerebral artery stroke

explanation.summary: Apoptosis is a normal, beneficial pathway that eliminates unneeded or self-reactive cells, whereas ischemic and thermal injury cause necrosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Apoptosis is a controlled, deliberate pathway with beneficial function to the organism. It works to eliminate immature lymphocytes with faulty machinery, such as those that could mount an autoimmune reaction against the body's own tissues. This physiologic deletion of self-reactive lymphocytes is a normal role of apoptosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bowel death from mesenteric ischemia results from loss of blood supply and is necrosis, not physiologic apoptosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cardiomyocyte death from coronary occlusion is ischemic necrosis, an uncontrolled and pathologic process.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A thermal burn is a physical injury that causes necrosis, not physiologic apoptosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neuronal death from a stroke is ischemic liquefactive necrosis, which is always pathologic.

questions.topicName: Cell Death: Apoptosis and Necrosis

questions.stem: A pathologist examines tissue and organs that were removed from patients during operative procedures, evaluating them under the microscope to diagnose disease and guide treatment selection. This work is the primary domain of which subspecialty of anatomic pathology?

explanation.summary: Surgical pathology evaluates tissues and organs procured by a surgical procedure.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines surgical pathology as the branch of anatomic pathology that evaluates tissues and organs procured by a surgical procedure, generated through biopsies, excisions, and resections. Evaluating operatively removed tissue under the microscope to diagnose disease is exactly this discipline.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytopathology focuses on diagnosis at the level of individual cells rather than intact tissues and organs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Forensic pathology and medical autopsy address cause of death, not routine evaluation of operatively procured tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hematopathology deals with blood products, which the brick specifically excludes from anatomic (and cytopathology) practice.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Molecular pathology involves specialized molecular tests for treatment selection rather than routine microscopic tissue evaluation.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: During an operative procedure for cancer, a surgeon notices a suspicious nodule in the mesentery. If the nodule is cancerous, the surgeon will alter the operation. Which of the following would be most helpful to rapidly determine the identity of the lesion during the surgery?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Excise the nodule for formalin-fixed paraffin embedding

explanation.summary: A frozen section provides rapid intraoperative diagnosis, usually in under 20 minutes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes the frozen section as a rapid intraoperative evaluation in which the pathologist freezes the tissue, evaluates it, and calls back a preliminary result, usually in under 20 minutes. This lets the surgeon obtain the identity of the lesion while the operation is still ongoing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Formalin-fixed paraffin embedding (FFPE) requires significant processing in the histology laboratory and is not a means of rapid intraoperative evaluation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Special stains are also performed on processed sections and cannot provide an answer during the surgery.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immunohistochemistry is generally performed on routine FFPE sections and would not be available until after laboratory processing.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Molecular testing may be performed in certain cases but takes significant time to yield results.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman has a suspicious cyst on her forearm. The surgeon removes the entire lesion in a single procedure, both to establish a diagnosis and to treat the patient by removing the abnormal tissue. Which of the following best describes this procedure?

explanation.summary: An excision (excisional biopsy) removes the entirety of the abnormal tissue and can be both diagnostic and therapeutic.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that excisions, including excisional biopsies, are performed with the intent of removing the entirety of the abnormal tissue, possibly curing the disease process. As such, an excisional biopsy can be both diagnostic and therapeutic and is less extensive than a resection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A core biopsy uses a needle to sample a core of tissue for diagnosis and does not remove the whole lesion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An incisional biopsy removes only a portion of the abnormal tissue for diagnostic sampling, not the entire lesion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A punch biopsy uses a cylindric blade to remove a small tissue sample, again for sampling rather than complete removal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A resection is a major surgery that removes part or all of an organ and is more extensive than an excision of a small cyst.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with gastric adenocarcinoma undergoes a major surgery in which the diseased stomach is removed. Which of the following terms names this resection?

explanation.summary: A gastrectomy is the resection of the stomach.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches resection terminology in which the procedure is named for the organ removed: a gastrectomy is a resection of the stomach. Resections are major surgeries often performed for malignancies such as gastric cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A colectomy is a resection of the colon, not the stomach.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A hepatectomy is removal of the liver.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A mastectomy is removal of the breast.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A nephrectomy is removal of a kidney and does not describe removal of the stomach.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: After a routine breast biopsy specimen is grossed, it is placed in fixative and processed by the histology laboratory into tissue blocks that are then stored for at least 10 years in case future evaluation is necessary. Which of the following best describes these archived blocks?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stained cytology smears on glass slides

explanation.summary: Routine surgical specimens are processed into formalin-fixed paraffin embedded (FFPE) blocks stored for at least 10 years.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that after grossing, surgical pathology specimens are typically processed into formalin-fixed paraffin embedded (FFPE) tissue blocks, and that these FFPE blocks are stored for at least 10 years in case future evaluation is necessary.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bronchoalveolar lavage is a cytopathology sampling method for cells from the airways, not a tissue-block preservation method.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fresh, unfixed tissue is not preserved and would not survive years of storage; the formalin fixation and paraffin embedding are what allow archiving.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Frozen section blocks are prepared for rapid intraoperative evaluation, not for long-term archival of routine specimens.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cytology smears are used in cytopathology to evaluate individual cells, not to embed and archive tissue blocks.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A tissue section is stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) for microscopic evaluation. Under the microscope, one of the dyes stains the nucleus and nuclear material a dark blue-to-purple color. Which dye is responsible for this staining?

explanation.summary: Hematoxylin stains the nucleus and nuclear material dark blue to purple.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that in the routine H&E stain, hematoxylin appears dark blue or purple and is useful for visualizing the nucleus and nuclear material, whereas eosin stains cytoplasmic components pink.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Eosin appears pink and stains cytoplasmic components, not the nucleus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver is a special stain that highlights fungal organisms gray-to-black, not a routine nuclear stain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immunohistochemical stains target specific molecular antigens (often appearing brown), not general nuclear material in H&E.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Masson trichrome is a special stain used to visualize fibrosis, not to stain nuclei in the routine H&E.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A 55-year-old immunocompromised man has a lung nodule, and the pathologist suspects a fungal infection. Which of the following stains would be most helpful to highlight fungal organisms in the tissue section?

explanation.summary: The Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) special stain highlights fungal organisms.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes special stains as dyes or chemicals with an affinity for a certain tissue component, and specifically states that the Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) stain is used to highlight fungal organisms, staining them gray to black.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Eosin alone stains cytoplasmic components pink and does not selectively highlight fungi.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immunohistochemistry for cytokeratin identifies epithelial (carcinoma) cells, not fungal organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Masson trichrome is a special stain used to visualize fibrosis, not fungal organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hematoxylin and eosin is the routine stain for general tissue architecture and is not the special stain used to highlight fungi.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A hepatologist requests evaluation of a liver biopsy to assess the degree of fibrosis (scarring). Which of the following special stains is most helpful for visualizing fibrosis?

explanation.summary: Masson trichrome is a special stain helpful for visualizing fibrosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists special stains and specifically notes that Masson trichrome is helpful for visualizing fibrosis, making it the appropriate choice for assessing the degree of scarring in a liver biopsy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Eosin alone stains cytoplasm pink and does not specifically demonstrate collagen deposition in fibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver is used to highlight fungal organisms, not fibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hematoxylin and eosin is the routine stain and is not the dedicated special stain for fibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immunohistochemistry for cytokeratin identifies epithelial-origin (carcinoma) cells, not areas of fibrosis.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A poorly differentiated tumor is difficult to classify on routine H&E. The pathologist performs immunohistochemistry, which is positive (brown) for cytokeratin, an intermediate filament found in epithelial cells. This result most strongly supports which of the following diagnoses?

explanation.summary: Cytokeratin positivity indicates epithelial origin, confirming a carcinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that immunohistochemistry directed against cytokeratins, intermediate filaments in epithelial cells, is often used to confirm a tumor as a carcinoma, a malignant tumor of epithelial origin. A cytokeratin-positive tumor is therefore best classified as a carcinoma.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Fibrosis is scarring visualized with Masson trichrome and is not a cytokeratin-positive epithelial tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A fungal infection is identified with special stains such as GMS, not with an epithelial immunostain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A lymphoma arises from lymphoid cells and is identified by lymphoid markers, not cytokeratin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A sarcoma is a malignant tumor of mesenchymal (connective tissue) origin and would not be defined by epithelial cytokeratin positivity.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A medical student wants to know the size of a hepatocellular carcinoma as measured in the pathology laboratory. In which section of the surgical pathology report would this information most likely be found?

explanation.summary: The measured size of a tumor is documented in the gross description.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the gross description is the physical description of the specimen and documentation of how it was processed, and that the size of the primary tumor (which determines the T stage) is found in the gross description.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An addendum details additional information after finalization that does not change the diagnosis, not the measured tumor size.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Clinical information may reference a radiologic size, but the size measured in the laboratory is recorded in the gross description.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The comment is where the pathologist gives an opinion on the case, not where the specimen measurements are listed.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The microscopic description details cellular and tissue-level observations under the microscope rather than the gross measured size.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: After a surgical pathology report has been finalized and signed out, an ordered immunostain result becomes available. It supports and does not change the original diagnosis. The pathologist incorporates this new result into the report. This addition is best described as which of the following?

explanation.summary: An addendum is a minor modification, such as incorporating later test results that do not change the diagnosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines an addendum as a minor modification to the report, such as the incorporation of testing results that were not previously available and do not change the diagnosis. That matches a supporting immunostain added after sign-out.

whyWrongByChoice.B: An amendment is a major change made after finalization; a change in diagnosis would warrant an amendment, which did not occur here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The final diagnosis is the top diagnostic line naming the disease, not a post-finalization addition of new test results.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The gross description documents the specimen's physical appearance and processing, not newly available test results.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A synoptic report is a structured report of prognostic information included in certain cancer cases, not a late modification.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman has a thyroid nodule sampled by fine needle aspiration (FNA), and individual cells are evaluated by cytopathology. Compared with a surgical pathology specimen, which of the following is a disadvantage of this cytopathologic approach?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It cannot be used to sample nodules of the thyroid gland

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is more invasive than a surgical resection specimen

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is not optimal for evaluating tissue architecture

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is unable to detect frankly cancerous cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: It requires removal of the entire affected organ

explanation.summary: Because cytopathology evaluates individual cells rather than intact tissue, it is not optimal for assessing tissue architecture.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that a disadvantage of cytopathology is that it is not optimal for the evaluation of tissue cytoarchitecture, and that fewer cells are available for evaluation compared with many surgical pathology specimens. FNA sampling of a thyroid nodule illustrates this limitation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: FNA is specifically described as commonly used for thyroid nodules and salivary gland tumors, so it can indeed sample thyroid nodules.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick lists minimal invasiveness as an advantage of cytopathology, so it is not more invasive than a resection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cytopathology can identify worrisome or malignant cells (for example, on a Pap smear), so it is not unable to detect cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cytopathology samples cells without removing an entire organ; whole-organ removal describes a resection, not FNA.

questions.topicName: Introduction to Anatomic Pathology for Patient Care

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man develops swelling and redness of the lower jaw 24 hours after a dental infection.
