A biopsy of the involved tissue is most likely to show an abundance of which cell type, given that these are the first cells to arrive at a site of acute inflammation and that their response typically peaks about 24 hours after injury?

explanation.summary: Neutrophils are the most abundant WBC and the first responders in acute inflammation, peaking around 24 hours.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neutrophils are the paramedics of acute inflammation and are the first cells to arrive at the scene. They are the most abundant white blood cells, making up about 60 percent of the total WBC count, and their response peaks about 24 hours after injury or infection. They kill microorganisms by phagocytosis and by releasing antimicrobial proteins.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Eosinophils are associated with parasitic infection and allergy, not the initial acute inflammatory response.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fibroblasts participate in later tissue repair and scarring, not the early acute inflammatory infiltrate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Macrophages become the predominant cell type only later, about 48 to 72 hours after injury, not first.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Plasma cells are antibody-producing cells of the adaptive response and are not the first cells at an acute site.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: Three days after a soft-tissue injury, the predominant leukocyte at the site is a large phagocyte that also takes up antigen, presents it to T and B lymphocytes, and secretes cytokines to help mount an adaptive immune response. Which cell is being described?

explanation.summary: Macrophages predominate at 48 to 72 hours, act as antigen-presenting cells, and secrete cytokines linking innate and adaptive immunity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Macrophages are leukocytes found throughout the body tissues that become the predominant cell type roughly 48 to 72 hours (2 to 3 days) after injury. Besides killing microorganisms and clearing cellular debris by phagocytosis, they secrete cytokines and act as antigen-presenting cells that help T and B lymphocytes mount an adaptive immune response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Basophils release mediators such as histamine but do not become the predominant phagocytic, antigen-presenting cell at 2 to 3 days.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Natural killer cells kill virally infected and tumor cells but are not the predominant phagocyte or the antigen-presenting cell described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutrophils arrive first and peak at about 24 hours; they are not the main antigen-presenting cell described here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Platelets contribute to clotting and release mediators but are cell fragments, not antigen-presenting phagocytes.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman scrapes her knee, and within minutes the surrounding skin becomes red and warm to the touch. These two cardinal signs are produced by the first vascular reaction of acute inflammation. Which change most directly explains the redness and warmth?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Clotting within the microvessels around the wound

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased local blood flow from vasodilation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Leakage of protein-rich fluid into the interstitium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Migration of neutrophils along a chemokine gradient

explanation.summary: Vasodilation increases blood flow to the injured area, producing the redness (rubor) and heat (calor) of acute inflammation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The first vascular reaction is an increase in vascular diameter (vasodilation), which increases blood flow to the injured area. Redness and heat are caused by this increase in local blood flow, making them among the earliest visible cardinal signs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Clotting in the microvessels helps contain infection but does not produce the redness and heat.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Leakage of protein-rich fluid causes swelling (tumor), not primarily the redness and warmth.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutrophil migration along a chemokine gradient recruits cells but is not the cause of the warmth and redness.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sloughing of necrotic tissue describes ulceration, a morphologic pattern, not the mechanism of redness and heat.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A patient develops visible swelling of a finger after a small puncture wound. The swelling results from accumulation of fluid and protein in the interstitial space. Which of the following is most directly responsible for this fluid accumulation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deposition of fibrin within the extracellular space

choices.label: B
choices.text: Diapedesis of leukocytes across the vessel wall

choices.label: C
choices.text: Expression of adhesion molecules on the endothelial surface

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vasoconstriction that reduces blood flow to the area

explanation.summary: Increased vascular permeability lets fluid and molecules leave the vessel, producing swelling (tumor).
explanation.whyCorrect: In response to inflammatory stimuli, endothelial cells contract and widen the endothelial cell junction, increasing vascular permeability. This lets fluid, specialized cells, and molecules reach the site of injury, and the resulting accumulation of fluid in the interstitial space causes the visible swelling.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fibrin deposition characterizes fibrinous inflammation and is not the mechanism of the interstitial swelling here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Diapedesis is the passage of leukocytes between endothelial cells, not the primary cause of the edema fluid.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Adhesion molecule expression helps leukocytes stick to the endothelium but does not itself cause interstitial fluid accumulation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Acute inflammation causes vasodilation, not vasoconstriction, and reduced flow would not cause fluid to accumulate in tissue.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A student is asked to place the steps of leukocyte extravasation in the order in which a neutrophil leaves the bloodstream and reaches an infected tissue. Which of the following is the correct sequence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binding, margination and rolling, migration, diapedesis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Diapedesis, binding, margination and rolling, migration

choices.label: C
choices.text: Margination and rolling, binding, diapedesis, migration

choices.label: D
choices.text: Margination and rolling, diapedesis, binding, migration

choices.label: E
choices.text: Migration, diapedesis, binding, margination and rolling

explanation.summary: Leukocyte extravasation proceeds as margination and rolling, then binding, then diapedesis, then migration.
explanation.whyCorrect: Leukocyte extravasation involves four steps in order: margination and rolling (the cell moves to the vessel wall and rolls along the endothelium), binding (the cell is firmly stopped and fixed in place), diapedesis (the endothelial junction is pulled apart so the cell slips into the interstitium), and migration (the cell moves up a chemokine gradient toward the site).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Binding cannot precede margination and rolling, and migration comes after diapedesis, so this order is incorrect.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Diapedesis is the third step and cannot come first; the leukocyte must first marginate and bind.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Binding must occur before diapedesis, because the leukocyte must be firmly fixed before it squeezes between endothelial cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This reverses the true order; margination and rolling is the first step, not the last.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 6-month-old boy has a history of delayed umbilical cord separation, poor wound healing, and recurrent bacterial infections that characteristically produce little or no pus. Neutrophils are abundant in the blood but fail to accumulate at sites of infection. A defect in which of the following steps of neutrophil extravasation best explains these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Firm binding of leukocytes to the endothelium

choices.label: C
choices.text: Production of neutrophils in the bone marrow

explanation.summary: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency impairs the binding step, so neutrophils cannot firmly adhere and cross the endothelium to reach the tissue.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the binding step, adhesion molecules firmly fix the leukocyte to the endothelium. Patients with leukocyte adhesion deficiency have defects in this leukocyte adhesion, so neutrophils cannot fix in place, extravasate, and reach the site of injury. This leads to impaired wound healing, recurrent infections, and a characteristic absence of pus despite blood neutrophilia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Impaired complement opsonization is a different immune defect and does not explain the failure of neutrophils to accumulate at sites of infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neutrophils are actually increased in the blood, so bone marrow production is not the defect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The failure is in leukocyte adhesion, not in macrophage cytokine secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vasodilation is intact in this disorder; the problem is that leukocytes cannot adhere and leave the vessel.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: During the final step of leukocyte recruitment, a neutrophil that has entered the interstitium must locate and move toward the site of injury. This directional movement up a concentration gradient is driven by which class of mediators?

explanation.summary: Migration is guided by chemokines, whose concentration gradient directs leukocyte chemotaxis toward the injury.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the migration step, the leukocyte must locate and move toward the site of injury. This is facilitated by chemokines, chemical signals whose binding to receptors on the leukocyte surface promotes directional movement up the chemokine concentration gradient, a process called chemotaxis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Immunoglobulins are antibodies of the adaptive response and are not the chemotactic gradient that directs migration.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Kinins increase vascular permeability and cause pain but do not direct leukocyte chemotaxis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prostaglandins contribute to vasodilation, pain, and fever rather than guiding chemotactic migration.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Selectins mediate the earlier rolling step by tethering leukocytes to the endothelium, not directional migration through tissue.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with gram-negative bacteremia develops high fever and hypotension progressing to shock. These systemic effects are largely mediated by tumor necrosis factor, interleukin-1, and interleukin-6 released by macrophages. Which class of mediators is responsible?

explanation.summary: Cytokines such as TNF, IL-1, and IL-6 cause local endothelial activation and systemic fever, metabolic changes, and hypotensive shock.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cytokines (including TNF, IL-1, and IL-6) are produced by macrophages, endothelial cells, and mast cells. Locally they cause endothelial activation, and systemically they cause fever, metabolic abnormalities, and hypotension that can progress to shock, exactly the picture seen with severe bacteremia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Complement drives chemotaxis and membrane attack complex killing, not the TNF/IL-1/IL-6 systemic shock syndrome described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Histamine causes vasodilation and increased vascular permeability locally but is not the mediator of systemic fever and shock.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Leukotrienes increase vascular permeability and promote chemotaxis but do not produce this systemic fever and hypotensive shock.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prostaglandins contribute to vasodilation, pain, and fever but are not the TNF/IL-1/IL-6 cytokines named in the stem.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman with an insect sting rapidly develops a red, raised, itchy wheal as mast cells degranulate. The chief mediator released causes vasodilation and increased vascular permeability with endothelial activation. Which mediator is primarily responsible?

explanation.summary: Histamine, released chiefly by mast cells, causes vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, and endothelial activation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Histamine is a vasoactive amine released by mast cells, basophils, and platelets. Its principal actions are vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, and endothelial activation, which together produce the wheal and flare seen after mast cell degranulation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Albumin maintains plasma oncotic pressure and is not a mediator of vasodilation or permeability.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fibrinogen is a positive acute-phase reactant that aids clotting and repair, not the mast cell mediator producing the wheal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hepcidin regulates iron handling in macrophages and does not cause vasodilation or increased permeability.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transferrin is an iron-transport protein and a negative acute-phase reactant, not a vasoactive mediator.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with bacterial pneumonia has a lung biopsy showing alveolar spaces filled with a thick, protein- and cell-rich fluid containing abundant neutrophils that reduces the area available for gas exchange. Which morphologic pattern of acute inflammation does this represent?

explanation.summary: A neutrophil-rich, protein-rich exudate forming pus is the hallmark of purulent (suppurative) inflammation.
explanation.whyCorrect: An exudate contains protein and cellular elements and arises from increased vascular permeability that lets neutrophils enter the tissue. The buildup of leukocytes produces pus, defining purulent (suppurative) inflammation. In bacterial pneumonia, pus fills the alveolar spaces and reduces the area available for gas exchange.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fibrinous inflammation is characterized by fibrin deposition in the extracellular space, not by a neutrophil-rich pus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pseudomembranous inflammation refers to a debris membrane in the colon (for example, C. difficile), not alveolar pus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serous inflammation is a watery, protein-poor transudate, such as a skin blister, not the pus-filled exudate described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ulcerative inflammation is a local defect of a skin or mucosal surface from sloughing of necrotic tissue, not alveolar pus.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man after a myocardial infarction develops chest pain and a pericardial friction rub. At autopsy the pericardial surface is covered by a shaggy pink meshwork of fibrin. This finding is characteristic of which morphologic pattern, which typically involves the lining of body cavities?

explanation.summary: Fibrinous inflammation deposits fibrin in the extracellular space and characteristically involves body cavity linings such as the pericardium.
explanation.whyCorrect: When vascular permeability increases enough for large molecules such as fibrinogen to leak out, fibrinogen deposits as fibrin in the extracellular space, forming a fibrinous exudate. This occurs when vascular leaks are large or there is a local procoagulant stimulus, and it is characteristic of inflammation in the lining of body cavities such as the meninges, pericardium, and pleura.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Granulomatous inflammation is a chronic pattern with epithelioid macrophages, not the acute fibrinous pattern shown here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Purulent inflammation produces neutrophil-rich pus, not the fibrin deposition described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serous inflammation is a watery transudate, not a fibrin meshwork on the pericardium.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ulcerative inflammation is a surface defect from sloughed necrotic tissue, not a fibrinous exudate over a cavity lining.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman with an acute infection has laboratory testing. During acute inflammation, most plasma proteins made by the liver rise, but a few drop below their normal levels and are called negative acute-phase reactants so that amino acids can be conserved for the positive reactants. Which of the following is a negative acute-phase reactant?

explanation.summary: Albumin and transferrin fall during acute inflammation and are the negative acute-phase reactants.
explanation.whyCorrect: Negative acute-phase reactants are proteins that drop below their normal levels during acute inflammation. Albumin, the primary protein maintaining plasma oncotic pressure, is produced in lower amounts to conserve amino acids for the positive acute-phase reactants, making it a negative acute-phase reactant.

whyWrongByChoice.B: C-reactive protein is a positive acute-phase reactant that rises and helps recognize and eliminate pathogens.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ferritin is a positive acute-phase reactant whose serum level rises to sequester iron during inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fibrinogen is a positive acute-phase reactant that increases and promotes tissue repair and RBC rouleaux.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hepcidin is a positive acute-phase reactant that rises and acts as a gatekeeper for iron stored in macrophages.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Acute Inflammation (Part 1 of 2)

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with a 20-year history of poorly controlled rheumatoid arthritis undergoes synovial biopsy of a chronically swollen knee. The pathologist notes that the process has been ongoing for years rather than days. Which of the following morphologic features is most characteristic of chronic, rather than acute, inflammation?

explanation.summary: Chronic inflammation is proliferative and heals by fibrosis, unlike the exudative, neutrophil-driven pattern of acute inflammation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that chronic inflammation is proliferative in nature and that the body attempts repair by adding connective tissue, producing fibrosis and, at times, granulomas. Because damaged tissue cannot be repaired normally, fibroblasts secrete collagen that expands connective tissue, so healing by fibrosis is a hallmark of the chronic process.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A neutrophil-predominant infiltrate is the main cell pattern of acute inflammation; chronic inflammation is dominated by macrophages, lymphocytes, and plasma cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Acute inflammation begins within minutes to hours; chronic inflammation typically takes over about 48 hours after injury and lasts weeks to years.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pus and abscess formation are classic results of acute inflammation, not chronic inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vascular changes and edema are exudative features of acute inflammation, whereas chronic inflammation is proliferative.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has a soft-tissue biopsy taken 3 days after a penetrating wound that failed to clear. The infiltrate is now dominated by large mononuclear cells that phagocytose debris, secrete cytokines, and appear to be organizing the response into a walled-off collection. Which of the following cells is the predominant cell type at this stage and orchestrates the transition from acute to chronic inflammation?

explanation.summary: Macrophages become the predominant cell about 48-72 hours after injury and orchestrate the acute-to-chronic transition.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that macrophages become the predominant cell type approximately 48-72 hours (2-3 days) after injury or infection, kill microorganisms through phagocytosis, and secrete cytokines. They orchestrate the transition from acute to chronic inflammation and can form the 'wall' of a granuloma that isolates foreign substances.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Eosinophils are associated with allergic and parasitic responses and are not the predominant cell described here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fibroblasts secrete collagen during repair but are not the phagocytic cell that orchestrates the transition to chronic inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutrophils dominate the first 48 hours of acute inflammation, not the later organizing phase described here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Plasma cells produce antibody but are not described as the predominant cell that drives the acute-to-chronic transition.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 50-year-old sandblaster who has worked without respiratory protection for 25 years develops progressive dyspnea, and lung biopsy shows chronic inflammation with particle-laden macrophages. Which of the following mechanisms best explains how his occupational exposure produced chronic inflammation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A resistant intracellular microbe evades macrophage killing

choices.label: B
choices.text: Alveolar macrophages consume silica particles they cannot break down

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neutrophils rapidly clear the particles, resolving inflammation within days

choices.label: D
choices.text: Repeated mechanical wear exceeds the tissue's capacity to heal

choices.label: E
choices.text: The immune system mistakes lung cells for foreign antigens

explanation.summary: Inhaled silica is engulfed by macrophages that cannot digest it, keeping them in a chronic 'processing' state that sustains inflammation (silicosis).
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that with ongoing toxin exposure some particles simply cannot be destroyed; alveolar macrophages consume inhaled silica but cannot break it down, and these particle-filled cells release inflammatory signals that cause a chronic inflammatory disease called silicosis. Macrophages consuming indigestible substances get stuck in 'processing' mode, leading to chronic inflammation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A resistant intracellular microbe describes infectious causes such as tuberculosis, not silica dust.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brick emphasizes that these particles cannot be destroyed, so the response is prolonged rather than resolved within days.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mechanical wear exceeding healing describes persistent injury such as osteoarthritis, not inhaled-toxin exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Attacking self antigens describes autoimmune disease (e.g., sarcoidosis), not the indigestible-particle mechanism of silicosis.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man who recently emigrated from Russia is admitted to the intensive care unit with fulminant respiratory failure and multiorgan dysfunction. Despite aggressive antibiotics and supportive care he dies. At autopsy, the lungs contain numerous large granulomas with central areas of caseous necrosis. Which of the following is the most likely cause of these lesions?

explanation.summary: Caseating (necrotic) granulomas are the hallmark of infectious granulomatous disease, classically Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that M. tuberculosis is a highly resistant intracellular pathogen the body contains by forming granulomas, and that the granulomas seen in tuberculosis characteristically have a central necrotic (caseating) core with surrounding multinucleated giant cells. Central necrosis distinguishes these infectious granulomas from noninfectious ones.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Crohn disease can produce granulomas in the gut wall but is not the classic cause of large caseating pulmonary granulomas.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HIV promotes chronic inflammation by evading immune killing but does not itself form caseating granulomas.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sarcoid granulomas characteristically lack central necrosis (non-caseating), the opposite of what is described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Silica exposure causes silicosis with particle-laden macrophages, not caseating infectious granulomas.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 39-year-old woman presents with several months of dry cough, shortness of breath, and chest discomfort, and pulmonary function testing shows restrictive lung disease. Lung biopsy reveals well-formed granulomas containing multinucleated giant cells and lymphocytes but no central necrosis. Which of the following best characterizes this disorder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A non-caseating granulomatous process traditionally regarded as autoimmune

choices.label: B
choices.text: An abnormal passageway between two hollow organs or the skin

choices.label: C
choices.text: An infectious granulomatous process caused by a resistant acid-fast mycobacterium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lipid-laden plaque formation within the wall of a muscular artery

choices.label: E
choices.text: Scarring that replaces the liver's normal stromal framework

explanation.summary: Sarcoidosis produces non-caseating (necrosis-free) granulomas and is traditionally viewed as an autoimmune disorder, often causing restrictive lung disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes sarcoidosis as a noninfectious cause of granulomas that has traditionally been viewed as autoimmune, in which the body is tricked into treating its own cells as foreign. Sarcoid granulomas lack the central necrosis seen in tuberculosis and, when they accumulate in the lungs, lead to impaired respiration and restrictive lung disease with dry cough, shortness of breath, and chest discomfort.

whyWrongByChoice.B: An abnormal passageway between organs defines a fistula, not a granulomatous lung process.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An infectious mycobacterial granuloma (tuberculosis) shows central caseating necrosis, which is absent here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Arterial lipid plaques describe atherosclerosis, not a non-caseating granuloma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Liver stromal scarring describes hepatic fibrosis, not a pulmonary granulomatous disease.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man with long-standing Crohn disease develops recurrent urinary tract infections and is found to have an abnormal channel connecting a loop of inflamed bowel to the urinary bladder. Which of the following terms best describes this abnormal connection?

explanation.summary: A fistula is an abnormal passageway between two hollow organs or between an organ and a surface, a classic complication of Crohn disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines a fistula as an abnormal passageway between two hollow or tubular organs or between an organ and the body surface, most commonly in the GI tract. In Crohn disease, prolonged transmural inflammation drives fibroblasts to tunnel through the bowel wall; an enterovesical fistula between the GI tract and urinary bladder can present as recurrent urinary tract infections.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An abscess is a localized collection of pus, a feature of acute inflammation, not an abnormal channel.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An exudate is protein-rich fluid of acute inflammation, not an abnormal organ-to-organ passage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A fibrous cap covers the lipid core of an atherosclerotic plaque and is unrelated to a bowel-to-bladder connection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A granuloma is a walled-off mass of macrophages, not a passageway connecting two organs.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with a 6-month history of diarrhea and abdominal pain is found to have transmural, granulomatous inflammation throughout her GI tract and is diagnosed with Crohn disease. Her physician explains that one cell type coordinates the inflammatory response by releasing cytokines that alter the behavior of nearby macrophages and fibroblasts. Which of the following cells is most responsible for this cytokine secretion?

explanation.summary: T lymphocytes coordinate chronic inflammation by producing cytokines that reprogram nearby cells such as macrophages and fibroblasts.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the T cell's major role in chronic inflammation is the production of inflammatory cytokines that alter the behavior of nearby cells, including macrophages and fibroblasts. T cells react on antigen recognition and are central coordinators of the chronic inflammatory response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B cells give rise to plasma cells and produce antibody; the cytokine-driven coordination is attributed to T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Macrophages phagocytose pathogens and secrete cytokines too, but the brick identifies the T cell as the major cytokine producer that alters other cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neutrophils are the main effector cell of acute inflammation and are not the primary coordinators of chronic cytokine signaling.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Plasma cells secrete antibody, not the coordinating cytokines described.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A peripheral tissue biopsy from a patient with a chronic autoimmune disease shows numerous antibody-producing cells. On high power, each cell has an eccentric nucleus with coarsely clumped chromatin, deeply basophilic cytoplasm, and a pale zone beside the nucleus. Which of the following cells is being described?

explanation.summary: The plasma cell is a mature, differentiated B cell with an eccentric nucleus, clumped chromatin, blue cytoplasm, and a perinuclear hof.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes the plasma cell as a mature differentiated B cell that produces a specific antibody, and shows that it has a nucleus at the side of the cell (eccentric), characteristically clumped chromatin, blue cytoplasm, and a lighter space beside the nucleus called a perinuclear hof. In autoimmune disease, plasma cells make antibodies that target the body's own cells, driving continuous inflammation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fibroblasts secrete collagen and are spindle-shaped, lacking the described antibody-producing morphology.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Macrophages are large phagocytic cells that form granuloma walls; they do not show an eccentric nucleus with a perinuclear hof.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Multinucleated giant cells are fused macrophages within granulomas and have many nuclei, not a single eccentric nucleus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutrophils have multilobed nuclei and are cells of acute inflammation, not antibody producers.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with a long history of heavy daily alcohol use develops new-onset abdominal distention from ascites. Liver biopsy shows regenerating hepatocytes surrounded by dense bands of fibrosis. Which of the following consequences most directly results from these fibrotic bands?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complete restoration of normal liver architecture

choices.label: B
choices.text: Formation of caseating granulomas in the liver

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased resistance in the hepatic portal system

choices.label: D
choices.text: Narrowing of coronary arteries from lipid plaques

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rapid, reversible recovery of hepatocyte function

explanation.summary: Fibrotic bands in the liver raise resistance in the hepatic portal system, producing portal hypertension.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that chronic inflammation from alcohol damages the liver's structural framework so that regeneration is not possible and tissue is replaced by fibrotic lesions (scarring). It specifically states that fibrotic bands increase resistance in the hepatic portal system, causing portal hypertension, and that liver function is progressively and irreversibly reduced.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick emphasizes that once the framework is destroyed, regeneration is not possible and normal architecture is not restored.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Caseating granulomas are a feature of tuberculosis, not alcohol-induced hepatic fibrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Coronary artery narrowing from lipid plaques describes atherosclerosis, a different chronic inflammatory lesion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Liver function is progressively and irreversibly reduced, not rapidly and reversibly recovered.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with a long smoking history experiences sudden crushing chest pain and is diagnosed with an acute myocardial infarction. Angiography shows an occlusive thrombus overlying a disrupted atherosclerotic lesion. Which of the following best explains how chronic inflammation in the vessel wall led to this acute event?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A caseating granuloma eroded through the arterial wall

choices.label: B
choices.text: A fistula formed between two adjacent coronary arteries

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fibrosis of the myocardium regenerated the vessel wall

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neutrophils formed an abscess that occluded the artery

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rupture of the plaque's fibrous cap released lipids and mediators

explanation.summary: Atherosclerotic plaques are sites of chronic inflammation; rupture of the fibrous cap releases lipids and mediators that cause a thrombus, blocking the vessel and causing infarction.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes atherosclerosis as narrowing of arteries from lipid-laden plaques formed by the immune system's ineffective attempts to clear lipids in vessel walls damaged by smoking or diabetes, creating an environment of chronic inflammation. It states that rupture of the fibrous cap releases lipids and inflammatory mediators into the blood, forming a clot that can block the lumen and cause myocardial infarctions and strokes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Caseating granulomas are features of tuberculosis, not atherosclerotic plaque rupture.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A fistula is an abnormal passageway between organs, not the cause of thrombotic coronary occlusion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fibrosis produces scarring and loss of function, not regeneration of a healthy vessel wall.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Abscess formation is a feature of acute inflammation and is not the mechanism of plaque-related coronary occlusion.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A researcher studying a solid tumor observes that systemic chronic inflammation stimulates the growth of new blood vessels around the mass, providing an ideal environment for tumor growth and hematogenous spread. A drug is being developed to block this process and starve the tumor. Which of the following processes is the drug designed to inhibit?

explanation.summary: Angiogenesis, the growth of new blood vessels, can be driven by chronic inflammation and feeds tumor growth and metastasis; anti-angiogenic drugs block this.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes angiogenesis as the growth of new blood vessels in response to increased metabolic demand and explains that in cancer, systemic chronic inflammation leads to formation of new vessels around a tumor that feed it and provide an ideal environment for growth and hematogenous metastasis. It notes that drugs designed to inhibit angiogenesis are used to treat certain cancers by blocking the tumor's source of nutrients.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Caseous necrosis is the central necrosis of tuberculous granulomas, not a target for anti-tumor vascular therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fibrosis is collagen scarring; it is a separate consequence of chronic inflammation and not the vessel-forming process being blocked.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Isotype switching is a change in antibody class and is unrelated to tumor vascularization.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Phagocytosis is engulfment of particles by macrophages, not the formation of tumor-feeding blood vessels.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with a decades-long smoking history develops a chronic productive cough and progressive airflow obstruction. Biopsy of the airways shows thickened walls with luminal narrowing that obstructs airflow, and arterial blood gas reveals reduced oxygen saturation with carbon dioxide retention. Which consequence of chronic inflammation best accounts for these structural airway changes?

explanation.summary: Tissue remodeling from chronic exposure to airway irritants thickens the airway wall and narrows the lumen, as in chronic bronchitis, causing CO2 retention and respiratory acidosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that tissue remodeling occurs when chronic inflammation alters tissue structure to suit the inflammatory environment. It gives the example of chronic exposure to airborne irritants such as cigarette smoke leading to chronic bronchitis, in which persistent inflammation thickens the airway and narrows the lumen, obstructing airflow; the end result is reduced oxygen saturation and increased carbon dioxide retention that can cause respiratory acidosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Abscess formation is a localized pus collection of acute inflammation, not chronic structural airway remodeling.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Angiogenesis is the growth of new blood vessels, not the airway-wall thickening and luminal narrowing described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Caseating granulomas are features of tuberculosis and do not explain diffuse airway wall thickening from smoking.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Portal hypertension results from hepatic fibrosis, not from remodeling of the airways.

questions.topicName: The Inflammatory Response: Chronic Inflammation (Part 2 of 2)

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man survives a large anterior myocardial infarction. Several weeks later, the infarcted region of myocardium has been replaced by a dense collagenous scar rather than by new cardiac muscle, because cardiac myocytes are permanent (nondividing) cells. Which of the following cell types shares this same regenerative classification?

explanation.summary: Permanent (nondividing) tissues such as cardiac muscle and neurons cannot regenerate and heal only by scarring.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neurons, like cardiac myocytes, are permanent tissue: they are nondividing and lack the ability to regenerate, so lost cells are replaced by connective tissue scar rather than by new functional cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Basal keratinocytes of the skin are labile tissue that continuously divide to renew the epidermis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hematopoietic precursors of the bone marrow are labile tissue that divide continuously.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Colonic surface epithelium is labile (continuously dividing) tissue that regenerates readily when the ECM is intact.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hepatocytes are stable (quiescent) tissue that can regenerate once primed to re-enter the cell cycle.

questions.topicName: Wound Healing and Tissue Repair

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman undergoes colonoscopy with biopsy of the colonic mucosa. Two weeks later the biopsy site has fully regenerated with normal, functioning epithelium and no scar. Which property of colonic epithelium best explains this complete regeneration?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a labile tissue whose cells continuously divide

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a permanent tissue that heals only by scarring

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a stable tissue that must be primed before it can divide

choices.label: D
choices.text: It lacks an underlying basement membrane and extracellular matrix

choices.label: E
choices.text: It relies entirely on myofibroblast contraction to close defects

explanation.summary: Labile tissues are continuously dividing and regenerate completely when the extracellular matrix remains intact.
explanation.whyCorrect: Colonic columnar epithelium is a labile tissue that divides continuously; with an intact ECM/basement membrane scaffold it can fully regenerate the lost cells, restoring normal architecture without scar formation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Permanent tissues (e.g., cardiac muscle, neurons) are nondividing and heal only by scarring, unlike labile epithelium.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Stable tissues such as hepatocytes are quiescent and must be primed to divide; colonic epithelium divides continuously without such priming.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Epithelium sits on a basement membrane; this intact ECM is precisely what permits regeneration rather than preventing it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Myofibroblast contraction closes large open wounds by secondary intention; it is not the mechanism of epithelial regeneration.

questions.topicName: Wound Healing and Tissue Repair

questions.stem: A 45-year-old living liver donor undergoes resection of approximately 60% of his liver. Over the following weeks the remaining liver regenerates to nearly its original mass as hepatocytes leave a resting state and re-enter the cell cycle. Hepatocytes are best classified as which of the following tissue types?

explanation.summary: The liver is the classic stable tissue: normally quiescent hepatocytes must be primed to divide but retain a remarkable regenerative capacity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hepatocytes are stable (quiescent, G0) cells that do not divide continuously; following injury or loss they are primed by signals such as HGF and move from G0 into the proliferating G1 stage, allowing the liver to regenerate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Granulation tissue is a temporary reparative tissue of fibroblasts and new vessels, not a hepatocyte classification.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The interstitial matrix is a component of the ECM between cells, not a category of tissue regenerative capacity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Labile tissues (e.g., gut epithelium, bone marrow) divide continuously without needing to be primed; hepatocytes are normally quiescent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Permanent tissues cannot regenerate at all; the liver's robust regeneration excludes this category.

questions.topicName: Wound Healing and Tissue Repair

questions.stem: An 80-year-old bed-bound woman in a nursing home develops a non-healing ulcer over the sacrum after prolonged, unrelieved pressure to the area. Examination shows loss of the overlying epithelium with underlying granulation tissue. Which of the following mechanisms best explains this chronic wound?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune destruction of the epidermal basement membrane

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excess collagen deposition confined to the wound margins

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reopening of a previously closed surgical incision

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sustained compression compromising local blood flow

explanation.summary: Pressure sores are areas of skin ulceration and necrosis caused by prolonged compression that compromises blood flow, typically in immobile patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sustained pressure over a bony prominence in a bed-bound patient reduces perfusion and oxygen delivery, producing ischemic necrosis and a non-healing ulcer with loss of epithelium and underlying granulation tissue.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autoimmune basement-membrane destruction describes blistering diseases, not a compression-related pressure sore.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Excess collagen confined to the wound describes a hypertrophic scar, not an ischemic ulcer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Myofibroblast contraction produces contractures over joints, not a sacral pressure ulcer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reopening of a closed incision defines wound dehiscence, a postsurgical complication.

questions.topicName: Wound Healing and Tissue Repair

questions.stem: During the later stages of wound healing, one growth factor both stimulates fibroblasts to synthesize collagen and extracellular matrix and dampens the inflammatory response so that it does not damage the healing tissue. Which of the following growth factors has these dual actions?

explanation.summary: TGF-beta stimulates fibroblast collagen/ECM synthesis while suppressing inflammation during the later, remodeling phase of repair.
explanation.whyCorrect: TGF-beta attracts fibroblasts and drives extracellular matrix and collagen deposition while suppressing acute inflammation, making it central to fibrosis and later-stage wound healing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: EGF stimulates epithelial cell proliferation and migration, not collagen deposition with anti-inflammatory action.
whyWrongByChoice.B: PDGF is chemotactic for inflammatory cells, fibroblasts, and smooth muscle and helps stabilize new vessels; it does not suppress inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: TGF-alpha stimulates epithelial cell proliferation (like EGF) and does not deposit collagen or dampen inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: VEGF stimulates endothelial proliferation and vascular permeability (angiogenesis), not fibroblast collagen synthesis.

questions.topicName: Wound Healing and Tissue Repair

questions.stem: Granulation tissue forming in a healing wound requires the growth of new blood vessels, and these new vessels are notably leaky. Which of the following growth factors is most directly responsible for stimulating proliferation of the cells that line these new vessels during angiogenesis?

explanation.summary: VEGF drives angiogenesis by stimulating endothelial cell proliferation and increasing vascular permeability.
explanation.whyCorrect: VEGF, produced by mesenchymal cells, directly stimulates endothelial cell proliferation and increases vascular permeability, supplying the new vessels needed by regenerating granulation tissue.

whyWrongByChoice.A: EGF acts on epithelial cells, not on endothelial cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-6 is a cytokine that helps prime hepatocytes and coordinates inflammation; it does not directly stimulate endothelial proliferation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PDGF recruits smooth muscle cells to stabilize newly formed vessels rather than directly driving endothelial proliferation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TGF-beta suppresses endothelial proliferation and migration to stabilize vessels and instead promotes collagen/ECM synthesis.

questions.topicName: Wound Healing and Tissue Repair

questions.stem: A large traumatic skin wound with extensive tissue loss heals by secondary intention. Over about 6 weeks the wound margins are drawn together, substantially reducing the size of the defect. Which cell type is most directly responsible for this wound contraction?

explanation.summary: Myofibroblasts are contractile fibroblasts that pull wound edges together during healing by secondary intention.
explanation.whyCorrect: Myofibroblasts are a specialized type of fibroblast with contractile ability; they form a network within granulation tissue and slowly draw the wound margins together, closing large defects over weeks.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ordinary fibroblasts synthesize and deposit collagen but lack the contractile machinery to close the wound.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Keratinocytes are surface epithelial cells that re-cover the wound; they do not contract it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Kupffer cells are liver macrophages that provide signals and phagocytose debris, not wound contraction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Macrophages clear debris and secrete growth factors but do not physically contract the wound.

questions.topicName: Wound Healing and Tissue Repair

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman sustains deep burns to both hands in a house fire. Several months later, the skin over her finger joints has become tight and taut, and she is unable to fully extend her fingers. Which wound-healing abnormality best explains her limited joint mobility?

explanation.summary: A contracture is an exaggerated healing response, common after severe burns, in which myofibroblasts tighten tissue across a joint and restrict movement.
explanation.whyCorrect: Contractures result from myofibroblasts contracting the healing tissue; when they occur over joints, especially after extensive burns, the skin becomes taut and leads to permanent limitation of joint mobility.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Dehiscence is the reopening of a closed surgical incision, not a burn-related tightening over joints.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A hypertrophic scar is excess collagen confined within the wound borders; it does not typically restrict joint motion the way a contracture does.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A keloid is exuberant scar extending beyond the wound margins, not a cause of restricted joint extension.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Venous ulceration is a chronic non-healing wound from venous hypertension, unrelated to burn-induced joint stiffness.

questions.topicName: Wound Healing and Tissue Repair

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman develops a firm, raised nodule at the site of an ear piercing. The lesion has grown well beyond the original margins of the piercing wound and has not regressed over the past year. Histology shows thick, brightly eosinophilic collagen bundles that are haphazardly arranged. Which of the following best describes this lesion?

explanation.summary: Keloids are exuberant scars whose thick, haphazard eosinophilic collagen extends beyond the original wound borders and does not regress.
explanation.whyCorrect: A keloid occurs when scarring extends beyond the boundaries of the original wound; microscopically it shows thick, brightly eosinophilic collagen arranged haphazardly, and unlike a hypertrophic scar it does not regress on its own and may require excision.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A contracture is tightening of healed tissue over a joint that limits motion, not a raised collagen nodule.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Granulation tissue is soft, pink, and temporary; a firm chronic collagenous nodule is not granulation tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A hypertrophic scar remains confined within the original wound margins and usually regresses over time, unlike this expanding lesion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Dehiscence is the reopening of a closed incision, not an excess scar.

questions.topicName: Wound Healing and Tissue Repair

questions.stem: Five days after a skin injury, the wound bed is filled with soft, pink, granular tissue that bleeds easily when a scab is lifted. Microscopically it contains proliferating fibroblasts, delicate new capillaries, and macrophages within loose extracellular matrix. Which of the following best identifies this tissue?

explanation.summary: Granulation tissue is the weak, pink, intermediate repair tissue of fibroblasts, macrophages, and new vessels that later matures into scar.
explanation.whyCorrect: Granulation tissue represents the intermediate stage of connective tissue repair; it is structurally weak and named for its pink, granular appearance, with delicate new vessels that bleed easily and proliferating fibroblasts that later deposit collagen.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The basement membrane is a thin specialized ECM layer supporting epithelium, not a bed of proliferating vessels and fibroblasts.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Caseous necrosis is cheese-like dead tissue typical of granulomatous infection, not vascular reparative tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A keloid is an exuberant collagenous scar extending beyond wound margins, not early reparative tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A mature fibrotic scar is a firm, pale, dense collagen structure that is the end result of remodeling, not soft pink granular tissue.

questions.topicName: Wound Healing and Tissue Repair

questions.stem: On postoperative day 6 after abdominal surgery, a patient's closed midline surgical incision suddenly reopens along the suture line. Which of the following terms best describes this complication?

explanation.summary: Dehiscence is a surgical complication in which a closed incision reopens.
explanation.whyCorrect: Wound dehiscence is a postsurgical complication defined by the reopening of a previously closed incision, typically when the wound has not yet gained adequate tensile strength.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chronic ulceration is a non-healing wound lacking intact epithelium, usually from impaired perfusion, not acute incisional reopening.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A contracture is exaggerated healing that tightens tissue and limits joint motion, not a reopened incision.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hypertrophic scarring is excess collagen within the wound borders, not incisional separation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A keloid is exuberant scar extending beyond the wound margins, the opposite problem of a wound coming apart.

questions.topicName: Wound Healing and Tissue Repair

questions.stem: An elderly man whose diet lacks fresh fruits and vegetables presents with poorly healing wounds, bleeding gums, and perifollicular hemorrhages. His impaired wound healing is attributed to deficiency of a vitamin required for collagen synthesis and blood vessel maintenance. Which of the following vitamins is deficient?

explanation.summary: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is required for collagen synthesis; its deficiency causes scurvy with bleeding and impaired wound healing.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ascorbic acid is necessary for collagen synthesis and blood vessel maintenance; its deficiency produces scurvy, typified by bleeding (gums, perifollicular hemorrhages) and impaired wound healing, historically prevented by citrus consumption.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Vitamin A supports epithelial differentiation and immune function but is not the collagen-synthesis vitamin whose deficiency causes scurvy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia and neurologic disease, not a collagen/bleeding syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vitamin D deficiency causes rickets/osteomalacia from impaired mineralization, not impaired collagen-based wound healing.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vitamin K deficiency causes a coagulation-factor bleeding disorder but does not impair collagen synthesis in wound repair.

questions.topicName: Wound Healing and Tissue Repair

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man who works in a wood-preservation and pesticide facility presents with several weeks of abdominal cramping, diarrhea, and tingling and numbness in his hands and feet. On examination his breath has a garlic-like odor, and transverse white bands are noted across several fingernails. Which of the following toxins is most likely responsible for his presentation?

explanation.summary: Arsenic exposure classically causes garlic-odor breath, gastrointestinal symptoms, transverse white nail bands (Mees' lines), and sensorimotor neuropathy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Inorganic arsenic is found in soil and water and is used in herbicides, pesticides, and wood treatment and preservation. It inhibits sulfhydryl-containing enzymes and interferes with the electron transport chain. Clinical clues include garlicky breath, gastrointestinal symptoms, a transverse white band across the nail bed, and neurologic effects such as paresthesias that can appear weeks after exposure.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Carbon monoxide is a non-irritating, odorless gas that binds hemoglobin and causes hypoxia, not nail banding or garlic odor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lead poisoning produces microcytic anemia with basophilic stippling, wrist drop, and a blue gingival line rather than garlic breath and Mees' lines.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mercury exposure comes largely from contaminated fish and dental amalgam vapors and causes neuromotor and cognitive dysfunction, not garlicky breath.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Radon is a radioactive gas whose main consequence is lung cancer, not an acute garlic-breath and neuropathy syndrome.

questions.topicName: Environmental Disease Part 1 of 2: Chemicals and Substances

questions.stem: A 39-year-old painter who has spent several months renovating a house built in the 1950s presents with fatigue, abdominal pain, and difficulty extending both wrists. A peripheral blood smear shows a microcytic anemia with coarse basophilic stippling of red blood cells. Which of the following best explains the anemia in this patient?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autoimmune destruction of red cell membranes

explanation.summary: Lead interferes with enzymes of heme synthesis, producing a microcytic anemia with basophilic stippling.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lead has high affinity for sulfhydryl groups and interferes with enzymes involved in heme synthesis, impairing hemoglobin production. The resulting microcytic anemia is accompanied by basophilic stippling, which represents aggregates of ribosomes and ribosomal RNA that precipitate because of the impairment. The wrist drop reflects lead-induced peripheral neuropathy in adults.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha-particle DNA damage is a feature of radon exposure and is linked to lung cancer, not this anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: There is no autoimmune hemolysis here; the findings and old-paint exposure point to lead toxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Carboxyhemoglobin formation is the mechanism of carbon monoxide toxicity and causes hypoxia, not a microcytic anemia with stippling.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thiamine deficiency in alcoholism causes Wernicke encephalopathy, not microcytic anemia with basophilic stippling.

questions.topicName: Environmental Disease Part 1 of 2: Chemicals and Substances

questions.stem: A 2-year-old child living in an old home with peeling paint is brought in for irritability, developmental regression, and vomiting. Imaging demonstrates cerebral edema, and the child is diagnosed with lead encephalopathy. Compared with adults, why are pediatric patients particularly prone to central nervous system injury from lead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Their blood-brain barrier is more permeable

choices.label: B
choices.text: They eliminate lead more slowly through Phase II conjugation

choices.label: C
choices.text: They express more superoxide dismutase in neurons

choices.label: D
choices.text: They have higher hepatic cytochrome P-450 activity

choices.label: E
choices.text: They have increased carboxyhemoglobin binding capacity

explanation.summary: The pediatric blood-brain barrier is more permeable, facilitating lead entry into the CNS and increasing neurotoxicity.
explanation.whyCorrect: In addition to greater absorption of ingested lead, the blood-brain barrier is more permeable in pediatric patients, facilitating lead toxicity in the central nervous system. Lead poisoning in children can cause cerebral edema, demyelination of white matter, and necrosis, leading to learning disabilities and delayed psychomotor development; high doses can cause blindness, seizures, coma, and death.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Slower conjugation is not the described mechanism; the key factor is barrier permeability and increased absorption.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Superoxide dismutase handles reactive oxygen species and is not the reason children are more vulnerable to lead.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Higher P-450 activity would relate to xenobiotic metabolism, not to the enhanced CNS susceptibility that comes from a permeable barrier.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Carboxyhemoglobin binding pertains to carbon monoxide, not lead neurotoxicity.

questions.topicName: Environmental Disease Part 1 of 2: Chemicals and Substances

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man is found unconscious in his car inside a closed garage with the engine running. He is unresponsive, and examination reveals a cherry-red discoloration of his skin and mucous membranes. Which of the following best explains the tissue hypoxia in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alpha particles generate free radicals in erythrocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin and blocks oxygen transport

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reactive oxygen species peroxidize cell membranes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sulfhydryl enzyme inhibition halts the electron transport chain

explanation.summary: Carbon monoxide has roughly 200-fold greater affinity for hemoglobin than oxygen, forming carboxyhemoglobin and preventing oxygen transport.
explanation.whyCorrect: Carbon monoxide is a non-irritating, colorless, odorless gas produced by incomplete oxidation of hydrocarbons. Hemoglobin has about a 200-fold greater affinity for CO than for oxygen, and CO binding forms carboxyhemoglobin, a stable form that prevents the binding and transport of oxygen. Acute exposure in an enclosed running car can cause coma within minutes, and cherry-red discoloration may be seen.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha-particle free radical generation describes radon toxicity, not carbon monoxide poisoning.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nicotine vasoconstriction impairs wound healing but does not produce carboxyhemoglobin or cherry-red skin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Membrane lipid peroxidation from ROS is a feature of alcohol and radiation injury, not the CO mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sulfhydryl enzyme inhibition of the electron transport chain describes arsenic, not carbon monoxide.

questions.topicName: Environmental Disease Part 1 of 2: Chemicals and Substances

questions.stem: A 58-year-old lifelong nonsmoker is diagnosed with lung cancer. His home was found to have elevated levels of a radioactive gas derived from uranium in the soil. Which of the following best describes how this exposure damaged his respiratory epithelium?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alpha particles emitted during decay generate free radicals

choices.label: B
choices.text: It forms DNA adducts after activation by cytochrome P-450

choices.label: C
choices.text: It inhibits sulfhydryl-containing enzymes in the airway

choices.label: D
choices.text: Macrophages ingest the gas and release inflammatory mediators

choices.label: E
choices.text: The gas binds hemoglobin and starves cells of oxygen

explanation.summary: Radon decays into polonium and emits alpha particles that generate free radicals and reactive oxygen species, damaging DNA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Radon is a radioactive gas derived from uranium and is the number one cause of lung cancer among nonsmokers. It decays into polonium 214 and polonium 218, which cause ionizing radiation damage through the emission of alpha particles. Alpha particles release electrons that damage DNA, cells, and tissues through the generation of free radicals and reactive oxygen species.

whyWrongByChoice.B: P-450-activated DNA adduct formation describes tobacco smoke carcinogens rather than radon's ionizing radiation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sulfhydryl enzyme inhibition characterizes heavy metals such as arsenic, mercury, and lead.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Macrophage ingestion with inflammatory mediator release describes particulate matter, not a radioactive gas.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hemoglobin binding and oxygen starvation describe carbon monoxide, not radon.

questions.topicName: Environmental Disease Part 1 of 2: Chemicals and Substances

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man who worked in coal mining for decades dies of unrelated causes. At autopsy, his lungs and hilar lymph nodes show accumulation of black carbon-containing pigment. Which of the following terms best describes this finding?

explanation.summary: Anthracosis is the accumulation of carbon-containing black pigment in the lungs and lymph nodes after exposure to exhaust, tobacco smoke, and coal mining.
explanation.whyCorrect: Particulate matter, or soot, is produced by coal- and oil-fired plants, fossil fuel burning, and diesel exhaust. Ultrafine particulate matter is ingested by macrophages, and its accumulation as black carbon pigment in the lungs and lymph nodes following exposure to exhaust, tobacco smoke, and coal mining is termed anthracosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Angiosarcoma is a vascular liver tumor linked to vinyl chloride, unrelated to lung pigment.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Emphysema is irreversible enlargement of airspaces from tissue destruction, not pigment deposition.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mesothelioma is a malignant tumor associated with asbestos exposure, not benign carbon pigment accumulation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Silicosis is lung scarring caused by silica dust, not carbon-pigment accumulation.

questions.topicName: Environmental Disease Part 1 of 2: Chemicals and Substances

questions.stem: During Phase I metabolism of xenobiotics, cytochrome P-450 enzymes can generate superoxide, a reactive oxygen species. Which of the following enzymes is directly responsible for converting superoxide to hydrogen peroxide?

explanation.summary: Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide, a reactive oxygen species, to hydrogen peroxide.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick specifies that superoxide dismutase is responsible for converting superoxide to hydrogen peroxide. Both catalase and glutathione peroxidase are then capable of further processing hydrogen peroxide to water, a key step in detoxifying the reactive oxygen species that arise during xenobiotic metabolism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alcohol dehydrogenase metabolizes ethanol and has no role in superoxide detoxification.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Catalase acts downstream, converting hydrogen peroxide to water, not superoxide to hydrogen peroxide.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cytochrome P-450 is a Phase I enzyme that can generate reactive oxygen species, not detoxify superoxide.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glutathione peroxidase also processes hydrogen peroxide to water rather than converting superoxide.

questions.topicName: Environmental Disease Part 1 of 2: Chemicals and Substances

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man who spent 20 years working in a plant that synthesizes plastic resins develops a malignant liver tumor of vascular endothelial origin. Exposure to which of the following agents is most strongly associated with this tumor?

explanation.summary: Vinyl chloride, used to make polyvinyl chloride, is associated with hepatic angiosarcoma, a malignant tumor of vascular origin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Vinyl chloride is a chemical used in the synthesis of polyvinyl chloride resins used in packaging and building products. It is associated with angiosarcoma of the liver, a malignant tumor of vascular origin, which fits this worker's endothelial-origin hepatic malignancy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Asbestos is associated with mesothelioma and lung cancer, not hepatic angiosarcoma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Carbon tetrachloride is a solvent causing acute CNS depression rather than hepatic angiosarcoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Silica causes silicosis and is associated with lung disease and cancer, not liver angiosarcoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prolonged wood dust exposure is linked to nasal cancers, not a vascular liver tumor.

questions.topicName: Environmental Disease Part 1 of 2: Chemicals and Substances

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman who smokes one pack of cigarettes daily is scheduled for an elective procedure. Her surgeon strongly recommends smoking cessation beforehand, explaining that one component of tobacco smoke exerts vasoconstrictive effects that could compromise blood flow to the healing wound. Which component is he referring to?

explanation.summary: Nicotine exerts vasoconstrictive effects that reduce blood flow and impair wound healing.
explanation.whyCorrect: Impaired wound healing in smokers is attributed to decreased oxygen availability and the vasoconstrictive effects of nicotine, which limits blood flow to a healing wound. This is why smoking cessation is advised before elective surgery.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Carbon monoxide reduces oxygen availability through carboxyhemoglobin but is not the vasoconstrictive component.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nitrosamines are carcinogens implicated in cancer development, not vasoconstriction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Polycyclic hydrocarbons are carcinogens implicated in cancer, not the vasoconstrictive agent.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Radon is an environmental radioactive gas and is not a component of tobacco smoke affecting wound perfusion.

questions.topicName: Environmental Disease Part 1 of 2: Chemicals and Substances

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with a 40-year history of heavy cigarette smoking has chronic cough, phlegm, and progressive dyspnea. Autopsy of a similar patient shows irreversible enlargement of the airspaces due to destruction of lung parenchyma. Which of the following pathologic changes is most associated with tobacco use?

explanation.summary: Tobacco smoke destroys lung parenchyma, producing emphysema, the irreversible enlargement of airspaces.
explanation.whyCorrect: Emphysema is the irreversible enlargement of airspaces resulting from tissue destruction and is a component of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, which also includes chronic bronchitis. Tissue destruction by tobacco is driven by oxidative stress and pro-inflammatory effects, making emphysema the pathologic change most associated with smoking.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cherry-red discoloration of skin is characteristic of carbon monoxide poisoning, and would be unlikely in nonacute settings.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gingival pigmentation (a blue gingival line) is seen in lead poisoning, not tobacco use.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hemorrhagic mammillary bodies occur in Wernicke encephalopathy from thiamine deficiency in alcoholism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Macrosteatotic hepatocytes (fatty liver) are seen in alcohol use, not tobacco use.

questions.topicName: Environmental Disease Part 1 of 2: Chemicals and Substances

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man with chronic heavy alcohol use is found to have an enlarged, fatty liver on imaging, with hepatocytes distended by lipid. Which of the following metabolic changes from alcohol dehydrogenase activity best explains the accumulation of fat in his liver?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deficiency of thiamine impairing the citric acid cycle

choices.label: B
choices.text: Depletion of hepatic cytochrome P-450 enzymes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Formation of DNA adducts by acetaldehyde

explanation.summary: Alcohol dehydrogenase consumes NAD and raises NADH, and the reduced NAD availability shifts metabolism toward fat accumulation in the liver.
explanation.whyCorrect: Processing of alcohol by alcohol dehydrogenase reduces the availability of NAD while increasing NADH. Because NAD is needed for fatty acid oxidation and for converting lactate to pyruvate, this shift leads to accumulation of fat in the liver as well as lactic acidosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Thiamine deficiency causes Wernicke encephalopathy, not hepatic steatosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The MEOS pathway involves CYP2E1; alcohol does not simply deplete P-450 to cause steatosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Acetaldehyde-DNA adducts are linked to laryngeal and esophageal cancer, not the fatty liver mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vasoconstriction reducing blood flow is a nicotine effect on wound healing, not the cause of fatty liver.

questions.topicName: Environmental Disease Part 1 of 2: Chemicals and Substances

questions.stem: A newborn whose mother drank alcohol during pregnancy is noted to have a thin upper lip, a smooth philtrum, and short palpebral fissures, along with microcephaly and growth restriction. Which of the following mechanisms is most likely responsible for this clinical phenotype?

explanation.summary: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder results from apoptosis of developing fetal cells triggered by reactive oxygen species during acetaldehyde metabolism.
explanation.whyCorrect: A proposed mechanism for the teratogenic effects of alcohol is damage from reactive oxygen species produced during the metabolism of acetaldehyde to acetic acid, which in turn induces apoptosis, or programmed cell death, in developing fetal cells. This underlies the facial phenotype of a thin upper lip, smooth philtrum, and short palpebral fissures with microcephaly and growth restriction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder is an acquired teratogenic exposure, not an inherited single-gene disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The mechanism is programmed cell death (apoptosis), not uncontrolled coagulative necrosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Calcium metabolism dysregulation is seen in pediatric lead poisoning, not fetal alcohol effects.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Carboxyhemoglobin hypoxia relates to carbon monoxide, not the teratogenic mechanism of alcohol.

questions.topicName: Environmental Disease Part 1 of 2: Chemicals and Substances

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man is brought to the morgue after a fatal assault. The medical examiner notes a wound on the scalp that has irregular, ragged margins with strands of intact tissue seen bridging the depths of the wound. There is surrounding abrasion and contusion of the skin. Which of the following terms best describes this wound?

explanation.summary: Blunt-force tearing of skin produces a laceration with jagged edges and characteristic tissue bridging.
explanation.whyCorrect: A laceration results when blunt force overstretches and tears the skin. Because the tissue is torn rather than cut, the wound has irregular jagged margins and, diagnostically, intact strands of tissue (nerves, vessels) bridge the depths. Surrounding abrasion and contusion are common because the same blunt impact injures adjacent tissue.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An abrasion is a superficial graze that removes only epidermis; it does not have bridging strands.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A contusion is bleeding into tissue beneath intact skin, not an open wound with torn margins.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An incised wound is made by a sharp edge and has clean, straight margins with no tissue bridging.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A puncture wound is narrow and deeper than it is wide, produced by a pointed instrument, not a tearing force.

questions.topicName: Environmental Disease: Physical and Environmental Injury

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl is evaluated for possible abuse. Examination reveals several areas of skin discoloration over the back and buttocks that range from bluish-purple to yellow-green. The overlying skin is intact. Which of the following processes best explains these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A clean cut produced by a sharp edge

choices.label: B
choices.text: Coagulative necrosis from a thermal source

choices.label: C
choices.text: Removal of the superficial epidermis by friction

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rupture of small vessels with hemorrhage

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tearing of skin by an overstretching blunt force

explanation.summary: A contusion is hemorrhage into tissue from ruptured vessels beneath skin that remains intact.
explanation.whyCorrect: A contusion (bruise) is produced by blunt force that ruptures small blood vessels while leaving the skin surface intact. Extravasated blood is progressively broken down, so the discoloration evolves through characteristic colors; the range of colors here indicates lesions of differing ages, which raises concern for repeated injury.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A clean cut by a sharp edge is an incised wound, not an area of discoloration under intact skin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Coagulative necrosis from heat describes a thermal burn, which produces blistering or eschar, not evolving bruises.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Friction removal of epidermis describes an abrasion, which is an open superficial graze rather than subsurface bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tearing by blunt force describes a laceration, an open wound with jagged bridged margins.

questions.topicName: Environmental Disease: Physical and Environmental Injury

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man dies of a gunshot wound. On external examination, the medical examiner finds a round skin defect on the chest that is surrounded by a rim of abraded skin and a zone of surrounding soot deposition and punctate powder tattooing. Compared with the wound found on the back, this wound is smaller and more regular. Which of the following best characterizes this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A blast injury from an explosion

choices.label: C
choices.text: A distant entrance wound with no residue

choices.label: D
choices.text: A puncture wound from a knife

choices.label: E
choices.text: An exit wound produced at long range

explanation.summary: Gunshot entrance wounds are round with an abrasion collar; soot and stippling indicate a close firing range.
explanation.whyCorrect: A bullet entrance wound is typically smaller and rounder than the exit wound and is ringed by an abrasion collar where the projectile scrapes the skin. Deposition of soot and stippling (powder tattooing) around the defect indicates the muzzle was close to the skin, because these residues travel only a short distance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A blast injury produces widespread irregular fragmentation and burns, not a single round collared defect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A distant entrance wound would still have an abrasion collar but would lack the soot and stippling seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A knife produces a sharp-edged stab wound without an abrasion collar or powder tattooing.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Exit wounds are usually larger and more irregular than entrance wounds and lack an abrasion collar or powder residue.

questions.topicName: Environmental Disease: Physical and Environmental Injury

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man is pulled from a house fire. On the anterior chest and abdomen the skin is dry, white, and leathery in texture, and the affected areas are notably insensate to pinprick, whereas adjacent reddened blistered areas are exquisitely painful. Which of the following best describes the white, insensate regions?

explanation.summary: Full-thickness (third-degree) burns destroy the entire dermis and its nerves, producing painless, leathery, white eschar.
explanation.whyCorrect: A third-degree (full-thickness) burn destroys the entire epidermis and dermis, including cutaneous nerve endings, so the burn is painless (anesthetic). The devitalized tissue appears white to charred and leathery (eschar), and because the dermal appendages that regenerate skin are gone, these areas require grafting.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A contusion is subsurface bleeding under intact skin and is unrelated to thermal eschar.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A deep partial-thickness burn still spares part of the dermis and retains some sensation; it is not fully leathery and anesthetic.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A first-degree burn involves only the epidermis and appears red and dry but remains painful with intact skin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A superficial partial-thickness burn is moist, red, and blistered and is very painful, not white and insensate.

questions.topicName: Environmental Disease: Physical and Environmental Injury

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman is hospitalized with full-thickness burns over 40% of her body surface area. On the fourth day she develops hematemesis and melena. Endoscopy reveals multiple superficial gastric and duodenal ulcerations. Which of the following complications of severe burns does this represent?

explanation.summary: Severe burns predispose to acute stress ulcers of the stomach and duodenum, classically called Curling ulcers.
explanation.whyCorrect: Extensive burns cause splanchnic hypoperfusion and mucosal ischemia that lead to acute stress ulceration of the stomach and proximal duodenum, known as Curling ulcers. These superficial erosions can bleed, presenting as hematemesis and melena, as in this patient.
